# Research customers (parent)

## Purpose
This is the router for all customer research. It does not mine anything itself; it decides which source-specific sub-skill runs, in what order, and hands each one the same standing rule: nothing enters an avatar record without a source and a date.

## Steps
1. Read what the run needs: a general monthly sweep, or a specific open question a prior workflow could not answer.
2. For a general sweep, run reviews, tickets, social and onsite-behavior (all agent_does, no waiting on a person). For a specific gap, add interviews or surveys (human_assist, need a person to run them).
3. Route to each sub-skill by source. Each sub-skill owns its own connector, its own read pattern (star band, ticket tag, forum search, search-term log, guide, or questionnaire), and its own output shape.
4. If a connector for a picked source is not live (for example, no support desk export configured), mark that source unavailable in the packet rather than skipping it silently, so the founder knows a gap exists.
5. Return every sub-skill's packet, unmerged, to the calling workflow, which does the cross-source pattern check.

## Checks
- Every source that ran is named in the output.
- A source with no connector shows as unavailable.
- Packets are not merged or summarized here; that happens one level up, after cross-checking.

## Output
List of per-source packets: `{source, status: ran|unavailable, packet}`.

## Example
A monthly sweep for Gehna returns packets for reviews (12 tagged quotes), tickets (4 struggle themes), social (2 sub-avatar notes), and onsite-behavior (unavailable, no GA4 connector live yet).

# Mine reviews

## Purpose
Turn raw star-rated reviews into a tagged quote set and objection list an avatar record or copy brief can use directly, without re-reading the raw file.

## Steps
1. Export all reviews per SKU with star rating, date and marketplace (site, Amazon.com, Walmart Marketplace, etc.; Amazon.in, Myntra or another India marketplace where the brand sells there, markets: IN).
2. Group by star band. Read 1 and 2 star reviews for the real objection, which is often not the same as the stated complaint (a "poor quality" review may really be a fit or expectation-setting problem).
3. Read 4 and 5 star reviews for the job the product actually did in the customer's life, not just that they liked it.
4. Scan every band for identity markers: phrases like "I am a", "as a", "for my [relationship]" that reveal who is talking.
5. Prioritize long, narrative reviews over short generic ones ("nice product") for quote quality.
6. Discount a single contradictory review; only act on a pattern that repeats across multiple reviews.
7. Capture every usable quote verbatim, with SKU, star band, source platform and date. Strip the reviewer's full name.
8. Flag any use case mentioned that no competitor's marketing targets, as a candidate for BRAND-W08 (untapped avatar).

## Checks
- Every quote has SKU, star band, source and date.
- No full reviewer name is kept.
- A theme is only reported as real once it appears in 2 or more reviews.

## Output
`{quotes_by_star_band: [...], objection_frequency_list: [...], candidate_identity_markers: [...]}`

## Example
1-star band, 6 occurrences: "the strap felt flimsy after 2 weeks of daily wear" tagged as a durability objection, source: Amazon.com review, dated 14 Aug 2026.

# Mine support tickets

## Purpose
Support tickets are passive evidence of the customer's real struggle, separate from anything they said to make a sale. This skill turns that raw text into themes and support-macro material without exposing private customer data downstream.

## Steps
1. Export tickets, return reasons and call transcripts for the period from the support desk connector.
2. Tag each item by the underlying job or failure (a size mismatch, a delivery delay past the ZIP code's normal shipping window, a fabric-care confusion), never by the customer's exact wording alone.
3. Cluster repeated patterns; a single ticket is an anecdote, three or more with the same root cause is a pattern.
4. For each named, repeated objection, draft an update to the standing support macro that answers it.
5. Flag sizing, fit or fulfilment anxieties specifically, since these often feed a dedicated confidence angle in copy.
6. Log the consent status of every ticket before any quote leaves the ticket system; a ticket with no consent basis is summarized, never quoted verbatim.

## Checks
- Every quote used downstream carries a consent flag.
- Themes are tagged by underlying cause, not by the customer's literal words alone.
- Failed-delivery or regional shipping-delay patterns (and COD refusal patterns for India-market orders, markets: IN, null for US) are kept separate from product-quality patterns; conflating them misleads the avatar record.

## Output
`{struggle_theme_list: [...], draft_macro_updates: [...], quote_set_with_consent_flag: [...]}`

## Example
Theme: "sizing confusion, cross-body strap length" (9 tickets in 30 days) -> macro draft added: a strap-length chart link in the auto-reply for that product tag.

# Run social and forum listening

## Purpose
Public forums surface language, objections and sub-avatars in the customer's own words that a brand's own review file, which only hears from people who already bought, would miss entirely.

## Steps
1. Identify where this avatar actually talks in public: a subreddit, a Quora thread topic, Instagram comment sections on relevant posts, public Facebook groups.
2. Search those places using the avatar's own phrasing (from prior quote sets), not marketing terms.
3. Pull exact language, named objections, and any sub-avatar pattern (a distinct sub-group with a different job) that surfaces.
4. Record the source URL and date for every finding used.
5. Discard anything found in a private or closed group; only public, publicly-indexed content is used.
6. Flag any objection here that did not appear in the brand's own reviews or tickets; that gap is itself a signal (customers with this objection may not be buying at all).

## Checks
- Every finding carries a public URL and a date.
- Nothing from a private group, DM, or paywalled forum is used.
- Language additions are exact quotes, not paraphrases, since the language bank exists to reuse real words.

## Output
`{language_bank_additions: [...], sub_avatar_candidates: [...]}`

## Example
r/SkincareAddiction thread, dated 2 Sep 2026: "wish more brands made this in a travel size for humid weather" flagged as a sub-avatar candidate (frequent traveler) with 3 similar comments in the same thread.

# Mine on-site search and behavior

## Purpose
What a shopper types into the brand's own search bar, and what they browse but never add to cart, is a direct clue to the job they came to do, unfiltered by what the brand chose to say on the page.

## Steps
1. Pull on-site search query volume for the period, ranked by frequency.
2. Pull sessions that visited a category or product page multiple times without adding to cart, and note which page.
3. Cluster search terms into groups by apparent intent (a size question, a use-case question, a comparison question).
4. Flag any search term with meaningful volume and no matching product or content on the site; this is a direct unmet-demand signal.
5. Cross-reference high-volume browse-without-buy pages against the objection map, if one exists, to see if a known objection explains the drop-off.

## Checks
- Terms are deduplicated and ranked by volume before being called a pattern; one search is not a trend.
- A browse-without-buy pattern is reported with the specific page, not "the site" in general.

## Output
`{unmet_search_term_list: [...], job_clue_notes: [...]}`

## Example
Search term "cotton saree fall stitching" (41 searches, 30 days) with no matching product or FAQ content: flagged as an unmet demand signal for Product and Content.

# Run customer interviews

## Purpose
Passive sources cannot ask a follow-up question. When the research packet has a real gap, live conversation is the only way to hear the trigger moment or the fired alternative in the customer's own words.

## Steps
1. Write 8-12 open questions in job-to-be-done order: the trigger, the struggle, alternatives tried, the moment of choosing, the after-state. No yes/no questions, no question that names the brand's feature first.
2. Recommend a channel (phone, video call, SMS or voice notes; WhatsApp voice notes where the brand's customers use it, markets: IN, EU, LATAM) and a proportionate incentive sized against contribution margin, never cash large enough to bias the answer.
3. Recruit 8-12 people across at least 2 recency bands (recent buyer, lapsed buyer), never more than 70% from one band.
4. Hand the guide to whoever runs the calls (founder, team, or a research vendor); this step is human_assist, the agent does not conduct the call itself.
5. Log every transcript with a consent flag before any quote is reused.
6. Extract job statement material, the 4 forces, and the fired alternative from the transcripts, cross-checked against existing passive-data patterns.

## Checks
- No leading questions; no question that fishes for validation of an existing feature.
- Every transcript has a consent flag before reuse.
- Incentive cost is computed against contribution margin, not guessed.

## Output
`{interview_guide, transcript_log: [...], interview_findings_packet}`

## Example
Guide question 3: "Walk me through the day you decided you needed this: what was happening that day?" surfaces a holiday-gifting trigger moment absent from the review data.

# Run customer surveys

## Purpose
A survey is for confirming a pattern already found in reviews, tickets, social or interviews across a much larger sample. It is never the first place a new job or objection is discovered; fishing questions produce noisy, self-reported answers.

## Steps
1. Write the one claim the survey exists to test, drawn from an existing qualitative finding.
2. Pick the format: identity survey (who are you), post-purchase (why this, why now), or NPS/relationship (would you return). Keep to 6 questions or fewer, no double-barreled questions.
3. Draft the send in the email/SMS platform connector, which is read-and-draft only; it cannot send.
4. Founder reviews the draft and sends it themselves or approves the send explicitly.
5. Once the window closes, pull responses and drop straight-line or under-10-second junk responses, reporting the junk rate.
6. Score the confirm/deny result in code against the original hypothesis, with the real sample size shown, never rounded up to "most customers."

## Checks
- 6 questions or fewer.
- The survey confirms an existing finding; it never opens with "what do you want."
- No send happens without explicit founder approval.

## Output
`{survey_question_set: [...], cleaned_response_set, confirm_deny_result: {rate, n, hypothesis}}`

## Example
Hypothesis: "gifting is the top occasion for tier-2 city buyers." Survey of 40 questions sent to 600, 210 responses, 8% junk dropped: confirm rate 61% (n=193), reported as-is, not rounded to "most."

# Wild bet (parent)

## Purpose
This is the entry point and generic bounding procedure for any wild bet, before it is known whether the bet is a new product line, a new market, a licensing deal, a wholesale/retail entry, or a pop-up. It keeps the backlog alive and applies the same discipline (a real bound before launch) to every type.

## Steps
1. Every month, source wild bet candidates: adjacent-industry moves worth borrowing, category norms this brand could credibly break, and gaps the brand's own research (reviews, tickets, social) has surfaced. Log each with a date and the specific norm or gap it targets.
2. When a bet is proposed by the founder or pulled from the backlog for action, screen it against the brand's stated values and current team capacity before spending any more time on it.
3. Classify the bet's type. This determines which child skill runs next: `wild-bet/new-line`, `/new-market`, `/licensing`, `/wholesale`, or `/retail-popup`.
4. Once the child skill returns its type-specific feasibility packet, write the 8-field bound: hypothesis, the category norm broken, budget cap, downside cap (a share of contribution margin, computed in code, never guessed), cohort and size, control design, a specific stop rule, and a read-point date.
5. Flag for legal review whenever the bet promises something, sends mail or texts, or gates access to anything; default to "needs review" when unsure.
6. Hand the bound to the founder gate before any execution brief is written.

## Checks
- A bet conflicting with a named brand value is flagged, never silently bounded.
- Downside cap is a computed share of contribution margin, not an estimate.
- All 8 bound fields are present and specific before the bound is presented; a missing read point or stop rule blocks presentation entirely.

## Output
`{backlog_entry, screen_verdict, bet_type, 8_field_bound: {hypothesis, norm_broken, budget_cap, downside_cap, cohort, control, stop_rule, read_point}, legal_review_flag}`

## Example
Backlog entry, Sep 2026: "adjacent brand X ran a 48-hour founder-only pre-drop; this brand has never tried scarcity pricing": bet_type classified as new_line once proposed, routed to the new-line child for sizing before bounding.

# Wild bet: new product line

## Purpose
A new line is the most common wild bet type. The specific risk is building a full range before knowing anyone repeat-buys it; this skill keeps the pilot small and measurable.

## Steps
1. Run the market-sizing skill against the brand's own AOV, margin and repeat-buyer math for this specific candidate line, not the category in general.
2. Check the candidate against the current primary avatar's overlap: does the same customer buy this, or is this really a new-avatar bet in disguise (which changes the read entirely)?
3. Check with Product and Supply the smallest batch that can be produced and would still be a real test, not a token quantity that proves nothing.
4. Write the execution brief around a single pilot batch, sold to the smallest viable cohort by hand, with a named stop rule if the pilot does not sell through in the set window.

## Checks
- Sizing is computed in code from this brand's real numbers, not assumed from a category average.
- The pilot batch size is small enough to be a real test, not a full launch in disguise.

## Output
`{feasibility_packet: {sizing, avatar_overlap, batch_feasibility}, execution_brief}`

## Example
Candidate: a travel-size line for Gehna's existing jewellery avatar. Sizing shows 340 repeat buyers needed at the target price to hit contribution-margin breakeven; pilot batch set at 150 units sold direct via the existing list before any wider stocking.

# Wild bet: new market entry

## Purpose
Entering a new country or region carries regulatory, tax and logistics exposure a domestic wild bet does not. This skill front-loads exactly those checks so the founder decides with real constraints, not just opportunity size.

## Steps
1. Check what regulatory registration, import duty, or product-compliance requirement applies to selling into the target market (for example, a US FDA-adjacent labeling rule, or an EU CE-style requirement, depending on category).
2. Check the tax posture: for a new US state, sales tax nexus and registration thresholds on the home side; for a new country, US export treatment plus import duty, VAT (EU or UK) or GST on the destination side (GST applies only when the destination is India, markets: IN); state it in plain terms, flagging what needs a real accountant's sign-off versus what is a simple lookup.
3. Check who already competes there and at what price, so the entry is not blind.
4. Check logistics feasibility: realistic shipping cost and delivery time to that region, and how returns would even work.
5. Write the execution brief around the smallest reversible test (a limited SKU set, a marketplace listing rather than a full localized site) before any larger investment.

## Checks
- Regulatory and tax findings are specific to the named country, not assumed from general knowledge.
- Logistics costs are from a real quote or a published carrier rate, not estimated.
- The brief proposes the smallest reversible entry, not a full market launch.

## Output
`{feasibility_packet: {regulatory, tax, competitor_read, logistics}, execution_brief}`

## Example
Target: UAE. Regulatory check flags a municipality trading-license requirement for a local entity; recommendation is a marketplace-only test (Namshi/Noon) instead of a owned-site launch, pending that entity question.

# Wild bet: licensing deal

## Purpose
A licensing deal risks the brand's name and quality reputation in someone else's hands (or takes on someone else's IP under this brand's name). This skill checks the deal's economics and control terms before any negotiation.

## Steps
1. Research royalty norms for this product category and deal scale, from public deal reports or industry sources, dated.
2. Build a licensee (or licensor) scorecard: financial capacity to perform, fit with the brand's category and story, existing distribution reach, and any public quality-control or reputation history.
3. Draft deal-memo terms for the founder to negotiate from: royalty rate range, minimum guarantee, explicit quality-control approval rights on any product carrying the brand name, term length, and an exit clause if quality slips.
4. Flag legal review as mandatory for any licensing deal; this is never a bet the agent bounds without a lawyer's terms review.

## Checks
- Royalty norms cite a real, dated source, not a guess.
- Quality-control rights are explicit line items in the memo, not assumed to be standard.
- Legal review flag is always set to required for this bet type.

## Output
`{feasibility_packet: {royalty_norms, licensee_scorecard}, execution_brief: {deal_memo_terms, legal_review: required}}`

## Example
Proposed licensee scores strong on distribution (200+ retail doors) but weak on quality-control history (2 public recalls in another category); scorecard flags this as a founder discussion point before terms are drafted.

# Wild bet: wholesale entry

## Purpose
Wholesale changes the brand's margin structure and puts the product's story in someone else's retail environment. This skill checks the deal survives on the numbers before any buyer pitch goes out.

## Steps
1. Recompute unit economics at a realistic wholesale margin cut (commonly 50% off retail); check the deal is still profitable at the brand's real COGS, not the retail-margin COGS assumption.
2. Build the line sheet: SKUs offered, wholesale price per unit, minimum order quantity, and lead time, pulling MOQ and lead time from Product and Supply rather than guessing.
3. Build the buyer-facing pitch deck: brand story, positioning, sell-through data if any exists, and the line sheet.
4. Write the execution brief around the smallest real buyer commitment (one boutique, one small chain) as the pilot, before a broader wholesale push.

## Checks
- Wholesale-margin unit economics are computed in code from real COGS, not the retail-margin figure reused by mistake.
- MOQ and lead time come from Product and Supply's real numbers.

## Output
`{feasibility_packet: {wholesale_unit_economics, line_sheet}, execution_brief: {buyer_pitch_deck, pilot_buyer}}`

## Example
Retail margin is 55%; at a 50% wholesale discount, contribution margin per unit drops from $18 to $8: still positive, so the pilot proceeds with one boutique buyer at a 25-unit MOQ.

## Purpose
A retail pop-up or a new sales channel often fails on format and packaging fit before it ever fails on demand: a DTC-only box does not survive shelf handling, and a DTC price story does not survive a marketplace price-comparison page. This skill checks channel fit first.

## Steps
1. Decide which product format and packaging fits the target channel: a shelf-ready box for retail, a marketplace-compliant listing format, or the existing DTC format if the channel is another owned or partner site.
2. Brief the specific packaging and identity changes the channel needs (see `packaging-label-brief` for the mandatory-declaration side of this).
3. If this is a physical pop-up, size the activation to what the team can run by hand: staffing, footfall handling, and how sales get logged.
4. Write the execution brief sequencing packaging or listing changes before the buyer pitch or the activation itself; nothing launches in a new channel wearing DTC-only packaging.

## Checks
- Packaging or listing fit is checked against this specific channel's real constraints, not assumed identical to DTC.
- A physical activation is sized to real team capacity, cross-checked with `event-popup-design`.

## Output
`{feasibility_packet: {channel_fit, packaging_brief}, execution_brief}`

## Example
Target channel: a 3-day retail pop-up at a wedding expo. Packaging brief flags the DTC mailer box will not survive being carried by hand at a crowded venue; a compact gift-box format is briefed instead, reusing the existing brand palette.

# Job-to-be-done writer

## Purpose
An avatar defined as a job, not a demographic, is what makes the record useful for copy and product decisions later. This skill turns research patterns into a job statement that passes real tests, not a description that sounds insightful but cannot be used.

## Steps
1. Write the job in the form: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]." The situation must be specific and observable, not a mood.
2. Cover all three sides: functional (what gets done), emotional (how they want to feel), social (how they want to be seen).
3. Run the verb-noun test: the job should read as a verb-noun action a person can picture doing, not a trait.
4. Run the cross-category test: the same job should plausibly exist even if this exact product category did not, proving it is a real job and not a repackaged product description.
5. Name the 4 forces driving the switch: the push (the problem getting worse), the pull (the attraction to a new solution), the anxiety (what could go wrong with switching), and the habit (the pull of staying put). Each needs at least one verbatim supporting quote.

## Checks
- Statement passes both the verb-noun and cross-category tests.
- Every force cites a real quote, not an inferred feeling.
- No demographic detail (age, income) is substituted for the actual job.

## Output
`{job_statement, forces_record: {push, pull, anxiety, habit}}`

## Example
"When my sister's wedding date is set and I have 6 weeks to find jewellery that photographs well but doesn't look rented, I want a piece I can wear again after, so I don't feel like I overspent on a one-time costume." Push: rental pieces look fake in photos (quoted). Pull: seeing a real friend's photos in a piece like this (quoted).

# Objection map builder

## Purpose
An objection without a proven remover is just a complaint list. This skill pairs every named objection with the specific thing that actually removed it for a real customer, so copy and support both have something real to say back.

## Steps
1. List every named objection from the research packet, with its frequency count across sources.
2. For each objection, search the same research packet (and any product-change or policy-change log) for the specific thing that removed it for a real customer: a review that mentions the fix worked, a support reply that resolved a ticket, a policy change (like a size-exchange guarantee) introduced after the pattern was noticed.
3. Pair each objection with its remover; a remover is not valid without 2 or more quoted sources showing it actually worked.
4. For objections that repeat monthly, draft an update to the standing support macro that answers it directly.
5. Flag any fit, sizing, or delivery-confidence pattern specifically; these often deserve a dedicated confidence angle in copy (a size guide, a fit guarantee callout) rather than just a macro.

## Checks
- Every objection-remover pair has 2 or more quoted sources.
- A remover is something that already happened (a real fix, a real reply), never an invented solution the brand has not actually implemented.

## Output
`{objection_remover_pairs: [{objection, remover, sources}], macro_drafts: [...], confidence_angle_flags: [...]}`

## Example
Objection: "unsure if the chain length suits my height" (11 mentions). Remover: a length-guide image added to the PDP, after which 4 subsequent reviews mention using it successfully. Paired with 4 quoted sources.

# Avatar record builder

## Purpose
This is the single procedure that turns scattered research into the one record every other specialist cites, and the same procedure that keeps that record honest over time instead of going stale silently.

## Steps (build mode)
1. Pull the job statement, forces, fired alternative, objection map, 5W profile and trigger moment from the upstream skills and research packets.
2. Assemble them into one record with a full quote set attached to every claim.
3. Check the source-type count: at least 2 independent source types, with at least one first-party source (the brand's own reviews, tickets, or search data) if this is an existing brand with real customers.
4. Set the status flag: "confirmed" only if the source-count bar is met; otherwise "provisional," stated plainly.

## Steps (refresh mode, quarterly cadence)
1. Audit which briefs and pages have cited this record since the last audit.
2. Retrace whether the product still earns the win the record describes (has anything changed: price, formulation, competitor claims).
3. Check evidence freshness; anything older than 2 quarters is flagged.
4. If stale, route back to the research workflow for fresh evidence rather than editing the record from memory or assumption.

## Checks
- Every required field is present or explicitly marked missing, never silently invented.
- The status flag matches the real source count.
- A refresh never rewrites a field without new supporting evidence behind it.

## Output
`{avatar_record: {job, forces, fired_alternative, objection_map, 5w, trigger_moment, quotes, status: provisional|confirmed}}`

## Example
Refresh audit finds the objection map's "delivery delay" pairing cites a policy fixed 14 months ago that has since regressed (returns log shows the same complaint rising again); flagged for a fresh tickets-mining pass before the record is reused.

# Avatar ranking

## Purpose
Not every avatar candidate research surfaces deserves to become the primary. This skill applies a consistent, evidence-weighted score instead of picking whichever idea sounds newest or most exciting.

## Steps
1. List every avatar candidate surfaced this quarter, noting which run (reviews, social, untapped-avatar pipeline, etc.) found it.

3. Score each remaining candidate on estimated reach (against the brand's own traffic and customer data) and product fit (does the current product actually serve this job well), computed in code using `shared/rank-candidates`.
4. Rank candidates by reach x fit x evidence strength.
5. Recommend a primary, and name the top 1-2 runner-ups with why they ranked below the pick.

## Checks
- Every scored candidate cites 2 or more independent source types.
- Reach and fit scores are computed in code from real fields, not estimated in prose.
- The current primary avatar is re-scored fresh each cycle, not kept by default.

`{ranked_list: [{candidate, reach_score, fit_score, evidence_score, total}], recommended_primary}`

3 candidates scored; the current primary re-scores highest (reach 0.8, fit 0.9) but a sub-avatar from social listening (reach 0.3, fit 0.95) is flagged as a strong runner-up worth a dedicated segment record.

# Untapped avatar discovery pipeline

## Purpose
When every competitor claims the same avatar and the product has no new feature to differentiate on, the way out is often a different customer, not a different claim. This is a structured search for a real, unclaimed adjacent avatar.

- Every candidate job must be something the product can do today.
- A candidate with no found evidence at all is dropped, not carried forward "just in case."

# Category ladder and XY positioning map

## Purpose
No positioning claim should be written before the field it competes in is actually mapped. This skill covers both the ladder (every rung a shopper could pick) and the map (where every real alternative sits on the two axes that matter).

## Steps
1. List every rung of the category ladder: the category itself, sub-categories, every real product alternative, and doing nothing as a real option a shopper could choose.
2. List the real competitive set: every brand or option a shopper would actually compare against, including at least one indirect or adjacent-category alternative, not only obvious direct rivals.
3. Choose two axes for the map based on what the avatar record shows this customer actually weighs in a decision (never pick axes just to leave an empty, flattering corner for this brand).
4. Plot the brand and every alternative on the two axes, citing the specific fact from the competitor packet that placed each one.
5. Identify empty corners, then check each against real demand evidence before calling it an opportunity rather than a corner nobody wants.

## Checks
- Every plotted point cites a specific fact.
- Axes are drawn from the avatar record's real decision criteria.
- "Doing nothing" appears on the ladder.

`{category_ladder: [...], competitive_set: [...], xy_positioning_map: {axes, points}, open_corner_note}`

Axes chosen: "price" and "craft-story strength" (drawn from avatar record showing craft story outweighs brand-name recognition for this buyer). Open corner at high-price/high-craft-story is checked against review data showing real demand for handcrafted detail at this price band.

# Positioning statement

## Purpose
This is the single procedure for turning a mapped competitive field into the one line a shopper reads and believes, including the fallback path when the map shows every direct slot already taken.

## Steps
1. Answer the 6 positioning questions in writing: for whom, for what category, against what alternative, what benefit, why believe it, why now. Every answer traces to the avatar record or a verified fact.
2. Draft the 3-sentence promise: the change, the mechanism, the proof.
3. Cut the promise to the one differentiation line a scrolling shopper would actually read.
4. Run the fixed positioning checklist (clear, ownable, provable, durable, no disputed statistic); a fail on any item blocks moving forward until fixed.
5. If the XY map shows every corner already occupied, search for an unclaimed dimension entirely (a creneau), take the deliberate against-position relative to the category leader, or reframe the whole category around a frustration the avatar record already documents.
6. Where two framings are both credible, design a small test (an ad message test, a landing headline split, or an AI-persona pretest) before committing to one.

## Checks
- Every claim passes `shared/claim-check` against the claims tiers.
- The differentiation line fails the strip test if a competitor's name could swap in and it would still read true: a fail means it is not ownable yet.
- A checklist fail blocks presentation to the founder until resolved.

## Output
`{positioning_statement, promise, differentiation_line, checklist_result: {pass|fail, notes}}`

## Example
Differentiation line: "Jewellery you can wear the Tuesday after the wedding, not just the wedding day." Strip test: fails if swapped for a costume-jewellery competitor (still true for them too): flagged to sharpen further before founder review.

# Market sizing

## Purpose
An idea sounds bigger than it is until it is sized against this brand's actual AOV, margin and repeat rate. This skill does that arithmetic in code, every time, instead of letting an estimate happen in prose.

## Steps
1. Compute how many repeat buyers, at what purchase frequency, would sustain the business or the candidate line at this AOV and contribution margin. Use the metric contract fields directly; a missing field shows as unavailable, never assumed.
2. Search for an independent size signal for the specific niche: category search volume, a relevant subreddit or forum size, marketplace listing count, or a review-count proxy for comparable products. Every signal needs a URL and date.
3. Place the candidate on a matrix of price point against the customer count needed, to see whether this is realistically a volume play or a margin play, stated as a range rather than a false-precise number.

## Checks
- All arithmetic runs in code, never estimated in prose.
- A missing input shows as unavailable, never filled with an assumption.
- A sizing claim always cites the independent signal it is based on; a niche with no findable signal is marked "unproven."

## Output
`{sustaining_buyer_count, size_signal: {value, source, date}, matrix_placement}`

## Example
At AOV $65 and 28% contribution margin, sustaining an $18,000/month line needs approximately 220 repeat buyers per month at a 2x/year frequency; independent signal: category search volume flat over 12 months per Search Console, so treated as a margin play, not a volume play.

# Name screening and packaging

## Purpose
This skill covers both a full brand-naming screen and the lighter product/SKU/collection name screen, and carries the winner through to a presentable, packaged deliverable once cleared.

## Steps
1. Set the scope up front: a full brand name needs all 7 quality checks and a full deliverable; a SKU or collection name defaults to a descriptive, benefit-first title unless a real reason calls for a coined name.
2. Score every candidate on the 7 core qualities: distinctive, meaningful, memorable, brief, positive, extendable, protectable. Show all 7 scores per finalist, not a single blended number.
3. Test sound and syllable count by reading candidates aloud; flag acronym traps (unpronounceable or already-claimed initialisms) and generic-name traps (too descriptive to ever be ownable).

5. For brand scope only, once trademark/domain clearance comes back clean: write nomenclature notes (why this name, what it signals), a short brand story, and a tagline that passes the strip test.

## Checks
- Every finalist shows all 7 individual scores.
- SKU/collection scope defaults to descriptive naming unless a documented reason overrides it.
- A brand-scope deliverable is only packaged after clearance, never before.

SKU scope: candidate "Everyday Gold-Tone Hoops, 18mm" chosen over a coined name "Aura Hoops" since the descriptive title captures 3 real search terms found in on-site search mining.

# Trademark, domain and language clearance

## Purpose
A name that scores well on the 7 qualities can still be legally unusable or embarrassing in a target market's language. This is the free screening pass; a paid legal opinion or filing is a separate, human_assist step this skill only flags the need for.

## Steps
1. Search the USPTO trademark database (and international equivalents such as the EUIPO or an India registry for any export market) for exact and close matches in this product category.
2. Search "name + industry term" combinations for existing uses that a database search alone would miss.
3. Check domain availability (.com and the relevant local ccTLD) and social handle availability across the platforms the brand actually uses.

# Brand story and promise

## Purpose
The story and the promise are both meant to stay stable for years, so they get written once, carefully, from real material, not regenerated per campaign. This skill covers both since they are written and tested together.

## Steps

- No invented biographical fact; the founder confirms every detail in the story.
- Every claim in the promise passes `shared/claim-check`.
- Tagline candidates that fail the strip test are cut before presentation.

`{brand_story, promise, tagline_candidates: [...]}`

Tagline candidate "Jewellery that keeps its shine after the wedding" passes the strip test (specific to this brand's durability claim, backed by a site-approved claim tier) while "Beautiful jewellery for every occasion" fails (any competitor's name reads equally true).

# Voice sheet builder

## Purpose
Any writer or model needs a concrete, example-based reference to sound consistently like this brand. A list of adjectives ("friendly, bold, premium") does not achieve that; real liked and disliked examples do.

## Steps
1. If no voice sheet exists yet, set a plain default voice (short sentences, digits not spelled-out numbers, no jargon) so copy work is not blocked, marked clearly as a placeholder.
2. Collect Kevin's real liked and disliked copy examples, from past brand work or explicit reference material; never invent an example for the exercise.
3. Derive 4-8 traits from the pattern in those examples (for example: "direct, never salesy," "warm but not cutesy").
4. For each trait, write one real liked example and one real disliked example, plus a one-line rule a writer can apply without re-reading the whole sheet.
5. Build a one-page cheat version (traits and rules only) and a longer full reference (with the examples and reasoning) for deeper onboarding.

## Checks
- Every trait's liked and disliked examples are real and sourced, never invented to fit the trait.
- The default voice, once a real sheet exists, is retired, not left stacked alongside it.

## Output
`{voice_and_tone_sheet: {short_version, full_version}}`

## Example
Trait: "confident, not boastful." Liked: "This chain won't tarnish. We tested it." Disliked: "Our chains are the best in the industry, guaranteed to amaze!" Rule: state the fact, skip the superlative.

# Brand consistency and perception-gap audit

## Purpose
Drift compounds quietly: one off-voice email, one guideline-breaking ad, and within months the brand looks inconsistent everywhere. This skill catches it monthly, and quarterly checks the deeper question of whether the stated identity still matches what customers actually believe.

## Steps
1. Crawl key site pages (home, PDP, checkout) using `shared/surface-audit`'s method and check against logo rules, visual language and voice.
2. Check current live ad creative (via the public ad library, read-only) and recent email/SMS sends against the same rules.
3. Score each drift item by visibility and distance from the rule, computed, not gut-felt.
4. Quarterly: compare the positioning statement, voice sheet and claims against what reviews, social mentions and survey results actually say, quoting real customer language.
5. Classify each gap as the brand under-claiming (customers already believe more than the brand says) or over-claiming (customers do not believe what the brand claims); over-claims are the higher priority.
6. Draft a specific fix for each drift or gap item, naming the owning specialist (Site, Media, Creative) who would execute it.

## Checks
- Every drift item cites the exact rule it breaks.
- Every perception-gap note quotes real customer language, not a paraphrase.
- Over-claim gaps are ranked above under-claim gaps.

## Output
`{site_drift_list, ads_email_drift_list, perception_gap_note, fix_list}`

## Example
Drift: PDP hero image on a new SKU uses a font outside the type system (breaks Visual Language rule 2). Perception gap: guidelines claim "handcrafted," but 6 recent reviews describe the finish as "machine-perfect": classified as an over-claim gap, flagged high priority.

# Reputation risk monitor

## Purpose
Speed and accuracy both matter in a reputation moment: acting fast on a wrong fact makes things worse. This skill verifies before it drafts, and always routes to the founder before anything goes public.

## Steps
1. Watch public mentions and reviews for a sudden spike in complaint volume, a viral criticism, or a specific factual attack, measured against a real baseline rate, not a single loud post.
2. Verify the underlying claim against the brand's own records before drafting anything; state whether it is true, false, or partially true, with the evidence.
3. Assess how far the criticism has spread and how much real brand or revenue risk it carries, using actual reach numbers where available.
4. Draft a short holding statement that acknowledges the issue and states what happens next, making no claim the verification step does not support, and draft an escalation note naming who needs to see this and what decision they must make.

## Checks
- The spike is measured against a baseline, never triggered by a single post.
- The holding statement never claims more than the fact-verification step actually established.
- Nothing is posted, replied to, or sent without founder review, always.

## Output
`{spike_alert, fact_verification_note, draft_holding_statement, escalation_note}`

## Example
Spike: complaint volume on one SKU up 6x normal rate in 48 hours. Verification: a batch defect is confirmed against internal QC records. Statement drafted acknowledging the specific batch and a stated fix timeline, nothing broader claimed.

1. Check the candidate for direct category overlap; default to treating non-competitive brands as the safer fit.
2. Check narrative fit: does the collaboration tell a story either brand's customer would actually want, not just a co-marketing convenience.
3. Run a public reputation and controversy check on the other party before any agreement moves forward or any ambassador is onboarded; a flag here stops the process for founder review.
4. If screened favorably, draft what the collaboration would look like: format, duration, what each side contributes, rough terms, stating the specific customer value, not just brand exposure.
5. For an already-approved, ongoing relationship (a licensee, an active ambassador), re-run the reputation check yearly, on schedule, not only when a problem is already visible.

## Checks
- Overlap verdict is explicit: none, adjacent, or competing.
- A reputation flag halts the process until the founder reviews it.
- Ongoing relationships get a scheduled yearly re-check, not just a one-time screen at signing.

## Output
`{overlap_verdict, narrative_fit_verdict, reputation_check_result, collaboration_brief}`

## Example
Ambassador candidate screens clean on overlap and narrative fit; reputation check finds a 2-year-old public controversy unrelated to the brand's category: routed to founder for a judgment call rather than an automatic pass or fail.

# Event and pop-up design

## Purpose
The best in-person activation targets a real place the exact customer already gathers, sized to what a small team can actually run by hand, not a scaled-up event-marketing fantasy.

## Steps
1. Identify a real, checkable place or occasion the target avatar already gathers: a wedding expo, a college fest, a local market, a festival pop-up, drawn from the avatar record, not a generic venue guess.
2. Size the activation to what the team can actually staff and run, stating the exact number of people needed.
3. Design the specific format matched to the venue's real constraints: a sampling booth, a shop-in-shop pop-up, a small guerrilla activation.
4. Cost the activation (space, staff, materials, permits or vendor fees) and check it against the budget ledger before proceeding.
5. Define the read plan: the specific metric (footfall, samples given, codes redeemed, follow-on online sales in the days after) and the measurement date.

## Checks
- The venue or occasion named is real and independently checkable.
- The activation states exactly how many people are needed to run it.
- Budget is checked against the ledger before any commitment.

## Output
`{venue_candidate_list, sized_activation_concept, activation_budget, read_plan}`

## Example
Venue: a 3-day wedding expo in the brand's home city, footfall ~4,000/day. Activation: a 6x6ft sampling booth, staffed by 2. Read plan: redemption codes given at the booth, tracked against online orders in the following 14 days.

---
# Competitive intelligence: win-loss and battlecards

## Purpose
Real comparison language comes from people who actually chose between this brand and a named competitor, not from guessing what a competitor's customer probably thinks. This skill runs that research and turns it into something support can actually use.

## Steps
1. Pull a small sample of people who almost bought this brand and instead bought the named competitor, and people who chose this brand over that competitor.
2. Ask why, in their own words, using open questions that do not lead toward a feature the brand wants validated.
3. Verify every difference named against what is actually true today (price, feature, delivery time, policy), checked against a current, dated source, never against what used to be true.
4. Turn the verified differences into a short, internal battlecard support or the founder can use in a real conversation.
5. Distribute the battlecard to support with a version number, and refresh it whenever a named competitor materially changes price, features, or policy.

## Checks
- Every difference is checked against a current, dated source.
- The battlecard is explicitly internal-facing; it is never published externally as a comparison page without a separate legal and claim-check pass.
- Win-loss questions are open, matching the interview-guide standard, never leading.

## Output
`{win_loss_transcripts, verified_difference_list, internal_battlecard}`

## Example
Verified difference: "this brand's exchange window is 30 days vs the named competitor's 7 days" (checked against both brands' current live policy pages, dated). Added to the battlecard as a support talking point for a hesitant near-miss customer.

# AI-persona pretest

## Purpose
This is a cheap filter, not a substitute for real research. It catches obvious misses (confusing wording, an unintended reading, a flat concept) before money is spent on a real survey, interview round, or test, and it is never allowed to be mistaken for real customer signal.

## Steps
1. Check the budget ledger before running any paid pass.
2. Build the simulated persona strictly from the existing avatar record's job, forces and real quotes; never from a generic stereotype or an assumed demographic.
3. Run the persona against the messaging, naming or concept shortlist and record its reactions.
4. Use the pass only to flag obvious misses; never to rank or declare a winner among the shortlist, since this is simulated, not real, data.
5. State plainly that the planned real survey, interview or test round still happens; this pretest only trims the shortlist first.

## Checks
- The persona is built from real avatar-record evidence, never a stereotype.
- Every output is labeled "simulated, not a real customer" everywhere it is shown.
- The real research round is never skipped because of this pretest.

## Output
`{persona_brief, simulated_reaction_notes, flagged_misses_list, trimmed_shortlist}`

## Example
Pretest flags that tagline candidate B reads, in the simulated persona's reaction, as implying a health claim the brand cannot back: dropped from the shortlist before it reaches the real message test.

---
# Packaging and mandatory label brief

## Purpose
Packaging artwork has two jobs at once: carry the brand's visual language, and legally declare what the law requires for this product category and channel in the target market. This skill briefs both together so nothing goes to print missing a required field.

## Steps
1. Pull the dieline, net quantity, and any per-channel packaging constraint from the Product and Supply specialist's spec; never re-derive these from guesswork.
2. Apply the brand guidelines' palette, typography and logo rules (clear space, minimum size) to the dieline layout.
3. Place every legally required declaration for the target market. For a US-market SKU: net quantity and manufacturer/packer/distributor name and address under the FTC Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, the Care Labeling Rule for textiles, a Prop 65 warning where the product or destination state requires it, and FTC Jewelry Guides quality marks (karat, plating, filled) where the product is jewelry. For an India-market SKU (markets: IN, reads null for US): MRP, Legal Metrology details (net quantity; manufacturer, packer or importer name and address; month and year of manufacture; consumer care contact), BIS or hallmark mark where the product category requires it, and the EPR mark where applicable.
4. Check any additional channel-specific rule (a marketplace's own barcode or return-label placement requirement) beyond the general legal requirements, for each target channel.
5. Run the full completeness checklist against the layout; a missing mandatory field blocks sign-off, it never goes to print with a "fix later" note.

## Checks
- Every mandatory declaration for this product category is present and legible at its required minimum size.
- Channel-specific rules are checked individually, never assumed identical to DTC packaging.
- A missing mandatory field blocks sign-off outright.

## Output
`{layout_draft, declaration_placed_layout, completeness_checklist_result}`

## Example
New SKU going to a marketplace channel for the first time: completeness check catches that the Prop 65 warning field, present on the DTC box, was omitted from the marketplace-specific dieline draft: blocked until added.

Purpose: write body copy that opens on the dominant appeal, proves it in order
of evidence strength, and closes on one clear action, fit to the exact space
the placement gives it.

Steps
1. Open on the angle's one dominant appeal, stated as a specific outcome, never
   a generic greeting or a restated headline.

   CTA is cut, not softened.
4. Fit the text to the placement's real limit: a feed ad tolerates a short
   punch, a carousel card needs far less, a marketplace module has its own
   fixed character cap.
5. Score reading level in code and cut or simplify until it clears grade 10.

Checks: one dominant appeal, one CTA, no claim outside the cleared list, fits
the real space limit, reading level under grade 10.

Output: the finished primary text string, its word and character count, and
its reading-grade score.

Example: a mattress ad's primary text opens "sleep hot? this one breathes,"
then cites the one clinical measurement on file, then closes with "try it 100
nights, free returns" and a single Shop Now CTA.

no headline states a claim the paired image contradicts

Purpose: produce a real range of headline candidates, not three near-identical

Steps

   specific benefit named (speed, price, comfort, status) rather than just

2. Where a static image is already chosen, check each candidate against it:

3. Check every candidate's character count against the platform's current

4. Rank the full set and mark the top 3 to 5 as the ones to actually test,

buzz"), ranked by which best pairs with the chosen close-up product shot.

name: Hook bank
invoke_when: the copy needed is the opening line or opening 3 seconds of a cold video, VSL or static, before any full script is written
steps: Draft 8 to 20 hooks covering different opening mechanisms (question, bold claim, pattern interrupt, relatable scene).
Grade each hook on 5 criteria: clarity, relevance, novelty, specificity, credibility.
Multiply the top-graded hook into layered variants across audio, on-screen text and visual, for video formats.
Confirm no hook names the product or the offer, since a cold hook should earn attention before either.
Rank the bank and flag the top 3 to 5 for test.
checks: 8 to 20 hooks drafted before grading
no product name or offer in a cold hook
top hooks flagged with a grading reason
output: graded hook bank (8-20 hooks, each with 5 scores), top 3-5 flagged, with audio/text/visual variants for video
skill_md:
---
name: write-copy/hooks
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: the copy needed is an opening line, before hook rate, for cold
  video, VSL or static formats
inputs: angle brief, past hook grades, product facts
outputs: graded hook bank with variants
---
Purpose: produce and grade enough real hook variety that a genuinely strong
opening survives the cut, rather than shipping the first idea that came to
mind.

Steps
1. Draft 8 to 20 hooks spanning different opening mechanisms: a direct
   question, a bold or surprising claim, a pattern interrupt (visual or
   verbal), and a relatable scene the viewer recognizes.
2. Grade every hook on 5 criteria: clarity (understood in one read), relevance
   (matches the persona's real problem), novelty (not the account's own
   overused opener), specificity (a real detail, not a vague promise) and
   credibility (believable without proof yet shown).
3. For video, take the top-graded hook and build layered variants: a different
   audio delivery, a different on-screen text treatment, a different opening
   visual, so one strong idea gets 3 or 4 real chances to test.
4. Check that no hook names the product or the offer; a cold hook earns the
   next 3 seconds first.
5. Rank the full bank and flag the top 3 to 5 with the reason they ranked
   there.

Checks: 8-20 hooks before grading; every hook scored on all 5 criteria; no
premature product/offer name.

Output: the graded bank, angle-tagged, format-tagged, with the top hooks
flagged and video variants attached.

Example: for a scalp-serum brand, hooks span "why does my scalp itch by
noon?" (question), "your shampoo is the problem" (bold claim) and a silent
close-up of flaking that cuts before a word is said (pattern interrupt).

name: Video scripts and storyboards
invoke_when: the copy needed is a full scene-by-scene video script, for cold video, VSL, testimonial-style or synthetic-actor reads
steps: Decide if a full VSL is warranted or a short cold-video structure fits better, from the product's real education need.
Pick the skeleton: 7-part VSL, cold-video 7-beat (hook, bridge, mechanism, product, proof, objection, CTA), or testimonial structure.
Draft scene by scene: time, visual, on-screen text, voice line, purpose.
Storyboard the shot list sized to how it will actually be shot or generated.
Check claim-proof pairing: every claim in the script has its proof beat nearby.
Confirm a single CTA closes the script.
checks: CTA present and singular
no unverified claim
claim and its proof sit close together in the sequence
output: scene-by-scene script table plus storyboard shot list
skill_md:
---
name: write-copy/scripts
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: the copy needed is a full video script, cold video, VSL,
  testimonial-style, or a synthetic-actor read
inputs: angle brief, hook bank, claim tiers, the product's real education need
outputs: scene-by-scene script table plus storyboard shot list
---
Purpose: script video ads in a proven, sized structure, never longer than the
product's real education need justifies, with every claim paired to its proof.

Steps
1. Decide the format length from the product's real complexity: a simple
   impulse product rarely needs a full VSL; a high-consideration or
   unfamiliar-mechanism product often does.
2. Pick the skeleton: the 7-part VSL for longer education, the cold-video
   7-beat (hook, bridge, mechanism, product, proof, objection, CTA) for
   shorter formats, or a testimonial structure built around a real customer

3. Write scene by scene as a table: timestamp, what's on screen, any on-screen

4. Storyboard the shot list, sized to whether this will be a real shoot, a

5. Check claim-proof pairing: every claim made has its proof beat within a

6. Confirm exactly one CTA closes the script.

not a habit.

Output: the scene table and the storyboard, both tagged to the angle and
format they serve.

Example: a water-filter VSL spends 20 seconds on the contamination problem,
15 on the mechanism with a visual proof, 10 on a real lab result, then closes
on price and one CTA, rather than padding to a fixed runtime.

every format claim cites a real metric, not an impression

---
Purpose: assemble the research a new angle needs, using the brand's own
already-mined customer language and this account's own real recent results,
rather than a generic best-practice list.

Steps
1. Pull the current voice-of-customer packet from the brand brain, which the
   Brand Brain Keeper owns and refreshes; this skill does not re-mine raw
   customer data itself, it assembles what already exists for this decision.
2. Pull this account's own last 90 days of ad-level results and rank which

   "what's working now" should mean this account, not the category in
   general.
3. Tag every objection carried into the map with its real quoted source and a

4. Tag every format claim to the specific metric and window that backs it.
5. Flag anything in the pull that reads as a genuine surprise rather than a

Checks: source and date on every objection; metric and window on every format

Output: the objection map and the format scan, both ready to feed the

every reference is explicitly tagged signal only

Purpose: gather real competitor structure signal, cadence, layout and mood,
without ever crossing into using a competitor's actual text, logo, product or

Steps

2. Where the gallery's own set does not have enough range, call the Reference

3. Write a one-line reason each reference was pulled: what structural or mood

4. Mark every single reference as signal only, explicitly, in the handoff, so

name: Angle builder
invoke_when: a research packet exists and a small set of testable angles needs to be defined before any copy is written
steps: Write the one-sentence angle for one persona.
State the buying question the angle answers.
Pick the single dominant appeal (price, status, ease, fear-avoidance, aspiration).
Set the awareness stage the angle targets.
Check the angle against claim tiers before it leaves this skill.
Repeat to produce 2 to 4 distinct angle candidates.
checks: each angle names one persona, one appeal, one buying question
no forbidden-tier claim in any angle
output: angle brief: 2 to 4 angles, each with persona, appeal, buying question, awareness stage
skill_md:
---
name: angle-and-test/angle-builder
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: research exists and a small set of testable angles must be
  defined before any copy gets written
inputs: objection map, persona/avatar record, product facts, claim tiers
outputs: 2 to 4 angle candidates, each fully specified
---
Purpose: turn raw research into a small, genuinely distinct set of testable
angles, each disciplined to one persona and one dominant appeal, so a test
batch actually isolates what it claims to test.

Steps
1. Write the angle as one sentence for one named persona; an angle that tries
   to speak to two personas at once gets split into two angles instead.
2. State the exact buying question the angle answers, in the persona's own
   words where the research supports it.
3. Pick a single dominant appeal, price, status, ease, fear-avoidance or
   aspiration, and hold to it; an angle mixing two appeals is not one testable
   thing.
4. Set the awareness stage (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware,
   product-aware, most-aware) the angle is built for, since the hook, proof
   and CTA all depend on it.
5. Check the angle against the brand's claim tiers immediately, before any
   copy is written on top of it, so a bad angle is caught at its cheapest
   point.
6. Produce 2 to 4 distinct candidates this way, not near-duplicates of one
   idea.

Checks: one persona, one appeal, one buying question per angle; no
forbidden-tier claim.

Output: the angle brief, each candidate fully specified and ready for the
test-plan-builder or a founder-video argument outline.

Example: from an objection map full of "will this actually fit my small
kitchen," one angle targets space-anxious apartment cooks on the ease appeal,
answering "does this take up counter space I don't have."

name: Test plan builder
invoke_when: an angle brief is ready and the creative side of a test needs a hypothesis, pack size and pre-set win/kill rule
inputs_required: registry: past test sizes for this brand
steps: Write the hypothesis in one sentence: what changes, and what it should move.
Set a clean one-persona-per-ad-set structure so the test isolates the angle.
Size the pack from this account's own delivery volume, not a fixed generic number.
Set the winner rule and the kill rule before any script is written.
Set the minimum read window from the account's own delivery, not a calendar default.
checks: winner and kill rule exist before launch
pack size and read window both derive from this account's real traffic
output: test brief: hypothesis, pack size, winner rule, kill rule, minimum read window
skill_md:
---
name: angle-and-test/test-plan-builder
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: an angle brief is ready and the creative side of a test needs a
  hypothesis and a pre-set win/kill rule
inputs: angle brief, metric contract delivery volume, registry of past test
  sizes for this brand
outputs: test brief with hypothesis, pack size, winner/kill rule, read window
---
Purpose: fix the test's judgment criteria before a single script is written,
so no one is tempted to move the goalposts once real numbers start coming in;
covers the creative side of the test only; MEDIA owns the budget and delivery
mechanics of the same test.

Steps
1. Write the hypothesis as one sentence: which angle or hook change is being
   tested, and which specific metric it should move (hook rate, CVR, CPA).
2. Structure the test as one persona per ad set, so a result can be
   attributed to the angle, not blurred across personas sharing a set.
3. Size the pack, how many ad variants launch at once, from this account's
   own real delivery volume using metric-read, not a fixed "always test 5"
   rule; a low-volume account needs a smaller, cleaner pack.
4. Set the winner rule and the kill rule in the same sentence as the
   hypothesis, before any creative exists, so the eventual read has no room
   for a post-hoc rationalization.
5. Set the minimum read window from the account's own delivery, enough days
   to reach a meaningful sample, not a calendar habit like "always 7 days."

Checks: rules exist before scripting starts; every number in the plan is
computed from real account data, not a template default.

Output: the test brief, handed whole into the launch checklist step.

Example: hypothesis "the price-anchor angle beats the durability angle on
CPA"; pack of 4 (2 per angle) sized to the account's 40-purchase/week volume;
winner rule is CPA 20% below target at 50+ purchases per ad.

name: Audience spec handoff
invoke_when: an angle's persona needs to become a concrete targeting spec and be handed to the Media buyer, without CREA building or launching it
steps: Pull the persona's real traits: age range, interests, in-group language, past-attempt behaviors.
Translate each trait into a targetable field (age range, interest, behavior, lookalike seed).
Set exclusions: existing customers, brand-term searchers, any persona this angle should not reach.
Package the spec with the persona id and angle id attached.
Hand the spec to MEDIA as a structured request; do not build or launch an audience.
checks: every targeting trait ties to a line in the persona record, not a guess
exclusions are explicit, not assumed
output: audience spec record: age range, traits, exclusions, matched persona id, handed to MEDIA
skill_md:
---
name: angle-and-test/audience-spec-handoff
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: an angle's persona needs to become a concrete targeting spec for
  MEDIA, without CREA touching the ad account
inputs: angle brief, persona/avatar record, past audience performance
outputs: audience spec record handed to MEDIA
---
Purpose: translate a persona into age, traits and exclusions a media buyer can
act on, while keeping account-building and launch strictly on MEDIA's side of
the line.

Steps
1. Pull the persona's real, research-grounded traits: age range, stated
   interests, in-group language, and what they say they already tried and
   rejected.
2. Translate each trait into a field a targeting spec actually uses: an age
   range, an interest or behavior category, or a lookalike seed source; a
   trait that cannot translate honestly is left out rather than forced.
3. Set exclusions explicitly: current customers who should not see a cold
   angle, brand-term searchers, and any persona this specific angle would
   alienate.
4. Package the spec with the source persona id and the angle id so MEDIA can
   trace it back to the research behind it.
5. Hand the spec to MEDIA as a structured request and stop; CREA never opens
   an ads-manager targeting screen itself.

Checks: every trait traces to the persona record; exclusions stated, not
assumed; handoff is a request, not an action.

Output: the audience spec record, logged and sent to MEDIA.

Example: persona "budget-anxious new parent, 24-34" becomes age 24-34,
interest tags for baby-gear comparison content, lookalike seed from past
90-day purchasers, exclusion on existing customers and brand-term searchers.

name: Format economics comparison
invoke_when: a concept is set and the ad format still needs choosing, compared by expected profit per ad rather than ROAS alone
inputs_required: account's own cost-per-asset and format hit-rate history
steps: List the candidate formats the concept could run as.
Pull this account's own cost-per-asset and hit-rate by format.
Compute expected profit per ad per format: (hit rate x average result value) minus cost per asset.
Weigh the product's real education or demo need against the fastest-to-produce format.
State the decision with the number behind it.
checks: decision cites a computed number, not a stated preference
product's real education need is checked, not assumed satisfied by any format
output: format decision with the profit-per-ad comparison shown
skill_md:
---
name: angle-and-test/format-economics
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: a concept is set and the format still needs choosing, compared
  by real economics, not habit or ROAS alone
inputs: angle brief, test brief, product's education/demo need, account's own
  cost-per-asset and format hit-rate history
outputs: format decision with the comparison shown
---
Purpose: pick the ad format from this account's own numbers, since a format
with a lower hit rate but a much lower cost per asset can beat a flashier,
expensive format on real profit per ad.

Steps
1. List every format the concept could reasonably run as: static, native
   platform format, UGC video, founder video, carousel, catalogue.
2. Pull this account's own cost-per-asset and win-rate history by format,
   using metric-read; a brand-new account with no history falls back to the
   product's education need alone, stated as such.
3. Compute expected profit per ad for each candidate format: hit rate times
   the average result value of a winning ad in that format, minus the real
   cost to produce one asset in that format.
4. Weigh this against the product's real education or demonstration need; a
   product that needs to be seen in motion should not default to static just
   because static is cheaper, if the computed profit favors video anyway.
5. State the final decision with the actual numbers shown, not a preference
   dressed as a conclusion.

Checks: decision has a number behind it; product's real demo need was
checked explicitly, not skipped.

Output: the format decision plus the profit-per-ad table that produced it.

Example: static costs 1/5th of a UGC video to produce and hits 22% of the
time versus 30% for UGC; on this account's numbers static still wins on
profit per ad because the cost gap outweighs the hit-rate gap.

name: Concept brief builder

steps: Fill every fixed field: persona, angle, offer, destination, format, awareness stage.
Confirm the destination link actually matches the offer stated.
Confirm hook, image and copy plan all share one awareness stage.
Attach the reference set and claim sources used.

destination link matches the offer stated
one shared awareness stage across hook/image/copy
skill_md:

Purpose: produce the same fixed-field brief every time, so a designer, video
editor or creator always gets the same shape of instruction regardless of
which angle or format is behind it.

Steps
1. Fill every fixed field in order: persona, angle (one sentence), dominant

2. Confirm the destination link actually sells the offer stated in the brief;

4. Attach the reference set used (layout/mood only) and the claim sources

5. Return the brief only once every field is filled; a blank field is treated

Checks: no blank field; destination matches offer; one shared awareness

Output: the concept brief document, ready to feed the format-specific
production brief.

Example: brief for the "price-anchor" angle states destination as the

bundle discount."

name: Native platform format craft
invoke_when: the chosen platform is TikTok- or Reels-style and the concept must be written so it does not read as a paid ad
inputs_required: product's actual real trait to feature
steps: Pick a native format from the product's real trait, not a passing trend.
Write it in the platform's own editorial voice, pacing and on-screen text conventions.
Avoid a polished, brand-commercial look that breaks the platform's own feed pattern.
Check the format still carries the angle's claim and CTA, even inside a native structure.
checks: format picked from a real product trait, not copied from a trending format with no fit
claim and CTA survive inside the native structure
skill_md:

name: briefing/native-format-craft
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: the platform is TikTok- or Reels-style and the ad must not read

inputs: angle brief, the product's real feature-worthy trait, current

---
Purpose: fit the concept into how the platform's own users actually post,
picked from something real about the product, not a trend with no connection
to it.

Steps
1. Pick the native format (a POV, a "get ready with me," a quick-tip list, a
   duet-style reaction) from a real, specific trait of the product, for
   example a satisfying unboxing motion or a genuinely surprising use case,
   never a trending format bolted on with no fit.
2. Write in the platform's own pacing: shorter beats, native captions style,
   the on-screen text conventions real creators use, not a repurposed TV-ad
   script.
3. Deliberately avoid the polished, brand-commercial look; a rougher, native
   feel is the point, since it is what keeps the ad from breaking the
   feed's own pattern.
4. Check the angle's claim and the CTA still survive inside the native
   structure; native does not mean the ad forgets to sell.

Checks: format ties to a real product trait; claim and CTA present despite
the native wrapper.

Output: the native-format concept plus script or shot notes in the
platform's own voice.

Example: a phone-case brand's "drop test" becomes a native-feeling POV of
someone actually dropping their phone on tile, not a studio slow-motion ad.

name: Shoot and photo direction
invoke_when: a real product shoot is being run, or any AI-touched image needs direction so the product shown matches what ships
inputs_required: product facts: real dimensions, material, color, fit
steps: Set image-accuracy direction naming the exact product variant or SKU being shot.
Build the numbered shot list with angles and gaze direction toward the CTA.
Book studio/location/model within the approved production budget.
Get signed model and location releases before the shoot starts.
QA retouching or AI-touch against the real product for color, fit, scale and material.
File and version the checked frames.
checks: release on file before use
no retouch or AI-touch changes a fact-bearing detail
output: image-accuracy brief, shot list, QA'd final frame set
skill_md:
---
name: briefing/shoot-and-photo-direction
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: a real shoot is running, or any AI-touched image needs direction
  so the product shown matches what a customer actually receives
inputs: concept or founder brief, real product facts (dimensions, material,
