name: Google campaign architecture and brand split
invoke_when: a new Google account is being built, an audit found a structure problem, or the monthly brand/non-brand check is due
inputs_required: brand brain: catalogue, margin, brand terms
steps: Give every campaign exactly one funnel job; check for overlaps.
Default to one campaign per job; require a written reason for every extra split.
Run one campaign per country; never two locations in one PMax.
Split Shopping by margin tier only where margins spread widely across the catalogue.

Set the safe defaults on every new campaign: Sales objective, Purchase-only conversion goal, Search Partners and Display off, Presence location targeting, tablets and TV off unless device data says otherwise.
Always split brand from non-brand across Search, Shopping and PMax.
Exclude brand from every cold campaign with both a negative keyword list and a brand-audience exclusion.
Run brand on manual bidding or impression share, never conversion-based smart bidding, at a higher ROAS target than non-brand.
Check cold-campaign search terms for brand-term leakage; kill tiny orphan campaigns and roll their spend into the top campaigns.
checks: every campaign has one stated job and a written reason for any split
brand is fully separated and excluded from every cold campaign
growth is judged on non-brand alone
output: campaign architecture diagram + brand/non-brand split plan + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-architecture
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: new account, an audit flags structure, or the monthly brand check is due
    inputs: catalogue, margin, brand terms, prior audit
    outputs: architecture diagram, brand/non-brand split plan, change list
    ---
    Purpose: give every Google campaign one job, and make sure brand-name traffic
    never gets counted as growth.

    Steps
    1. Map every campaign to one funnel job; flag any overlap.
    2. Default to one campaign per job; a second campaign for the same job needs a
       written reason.
    3. One campaign per country; never mix locations inside one PMax.
    4. Set safe defaults on anything new: Sales objective, Purchase-only goal,
       Search Partners and Display off, Presence targeting, tablets/TV off.
    5. Split brand from non-brand everywhere it can run: Search, Shopping, PMax.
    6. Exclude brand from cold campaigns with a negative list AND an audience
       exclusion, not just one of the two.
    7. Put brand on manual bidding or impression share at a higher ROAS target;
       check impression share actually covers the brand name.
    8. Scan cold-campaign search terms monthly for brand leakage; merge orphan
       campaigns into the account's real structure.

    Checks
    - Every campaign traces to one job and, if extra, a written reason.
    - No brand traffic inflates the non-brand growth number.

    Output: architecture diagram, split plan, change list.

    Example: a PMax campaign is running for both the US and Canada -> split into two
    country campaigns with a written reason (currency and duty messaging differ).

name: Google Merchant Center and feed
invoke_when: Merchant Center needs setup or a disapproval fix, or the weekly feed-quality check is due
inputs_required: brand brain: policies, product catalogue, reviews
steps: Match Merchant Center business info exactly to the live site; enroll the 4 add-ons (remarketing, reviews, ratings, promotions).
Fix disapprovals before warnings turn into limited performance; never claim an identity attribute (e.g. small business) unless true by Google's definition.
Put the converting search term and product type first in every title, inside the first 70 characters; no keyword stuffing.
Roll out title or description changes in batches with a recorded baseline, never all at once.
Give every variant its own GTIN; never duplicate one product at several prices; run one feed per currency.
Refresh the feed at least every 6 hours; turn on automatic item updates for frequent price changes.
Use custom labels to carry margin, bestseller and stock priority into campaign structure.
Test lifestyle images against plain product shots; override auto-cropped Shopping images with a 4:5 supplementary feed.
Duplicate the feed into role-specific versions for Shopping and PMax where needed; work toward the Top Quality Store badge.
checks: business info matches the live site exactly
no disapproval sits unresolved past its warning window
title/description changes rolled out in batches against a recorded baseline
output: Merchant Center setup checklist + feed audit + title/description rewrite batch + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-merchant-feed
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: Merchant Center needs setup, a disapproval needs fixing, or the weekly feed check is due
    inputs: policies, product catalogue, reviews, current feed
    outputs: setup checklist, feed audit, rewrite batch, change list
    ---
    Purpose: keep the feed eligible, trustworthy and search-matchable, since a bad
    feed caps every Shopping and PMax result before bidding ever gets a chance.

    Steps
    1. Match Merchant Center's business info to the live site; enroll the 4 add-ons.
    2. Fix any disapproval first, before it becomes limited performance; never claim
       an identity attribute that is not true by Google's definition.
    3. Rewrite titles: converting search term + product type first, inside 70
       characters, no stuffing. Roll changes out in batches with a baseline.
    4. Give every variant its own GTIN; never duplicate a product at multiple
       prices; run one feed per currency.
    5. Refresh the feed at least every 6 hours; automate updates for frequent price
       changes.
    6. Tag custom labels for margin, bestseller status and stock priority.
    7. Test lifestyle vs plain images; supply a 4:5 image feed to beat auto-crop.

    Checks
    - No open disapproval past its warning window.
    - Every title change has a recorded baseline to measure against.
    - No duplicate GTIN, no duplicate product at two prices.

    Output: setup checklist, feed audit, rewrite batch, change list.

    Example: 12 SKUs are disapproved for a missing GTIN -> fix listed first, before
    any title rewrite batch goes out, since disapprovals cap everything else.

name: Google Shopping campaign management
invoke_when: the weekly Shopping optimisation loop is due, or a new account needs its first Shopping campaign
steps: Start a new account on Standard Shopping, not PMax; decline the PMax preselection.
Launch the first campaign on bestsellers only, in one ad group.
Pick a structure matching catalog size and margin spread; tier products by rolling performance with their own budget per tier.
Run the weekly loop: structure, bidding, negatives, products.
Prune products that spend and click but drag ROAS down.
Pull or de-prioritise a shared product when a competitor discounts it 20-30 percent.
Launch a new SKU on its own small budget and listing group, separate from the bestseller cold start.
Give Shopping the largest share of Google budget for consumer ecommerce; layer Standard Shopping beside PMax once PMax plateaus.
checks: bestsellers launch first, alone
the weekly structure/bidding/negatives/products loop actually ran
a new SKU never launches inside the bestseller cold-start group
output: Shopping structure plan + weekly optimisation log + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-shopping
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the weekly Shopping loop is due, or a first Shopping campaign is needed
    inputs: catalogue, margin, current Shopping structure
    outputs: structure plan, weekly log, change list
    ---
    Purpose: run the Shopping loop the way it earns money: bestsellers first, tiered
    by performance, pruned weekly, never buried inside PMax defaults.

    Steps
    1. On a new account, start Standard Shopping; decline any PMax preselection.
    2. Launch bestsellers only, in one ad group, first.
    3. Pick a structure sized to catalog size and margin spread; tier products by
       rolling performance, each tier its own budget.
    4. Run the weekly loop in order: structure, bidding, negatives, products.
    5. Prune products that spend and click without earning ROAS.
    6. Watch for a competitor discounting a shared product 20-30%; de-prioritise
       that product rather than compete on price blind.
    7. Give a brand-new SKU its own small budget and listing group.

    Checks
    - Bestsellers launched alone before the catalogue widened.
    - The weekly loop covered all four areas, not just bidding.
    - No new SKU diluted the proven bestseller group's data.

    Output: structure plan, weekly optimisation log, change list.

    Example: a competitor cuts price 25% on a shared bestseller -> de-prioritise
    that product in Shopping rather than match the price without a margin plan.

name: Google Search campaign management
invoke_when: the weekly Search optimisation loop is due, or new keywords/RSAs are needed
steps: Classify keywords by intent before bidding; group into single-theme ad groups, never one keyword per SKU.
Use exact match on proven converters; use broad match only with smart bidding and proof.
Write 7-9 RSA headlines from the brand's own offer and bestseller angle; lead with product, price or offer; use descriptions to answer the real objection.
Fix quality signals before raising a bid; send cold, problem-aware traffic to an educational page, not a bare buy box.
Review search terms on a cadence that tightens for new campaigns and loosens once stable; remove clicked non-converters, promote converting broad terms to exact.
Build the account-level negative list at the right level, without blocking real product searches; turn off Search Partners and Display on every Search campaign.
Run DSA only with a large, multi-category content site, after RSAs already run; test AI Max for Search only on a cold, brand-excluded campaign.
Test landing pages from Search continuously with a duplicate ad rotation.
checks: keywords grouped by intent into single-theme ad groups
RSAs answer a real objection, not just describe the product
the negative list blocks junk without blocking real product searches
output: keyword/RSA plan + search term cleanup log + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-search
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the weekly Search loop is due, or new keywords/RSAs are needed
    inputs: offers, catalogue, current search-term report
    outputs: keyword/RSA plan, cleanup log, change list
    ---
    Purpose: bid only on proven or well-classified intent, and write ads that
    answer the real objection instead of just naming the product.

    Steps
    1. Classify keywords by intent; group into single-theme ad groups.
    2. Exact match on proven converters; broad match only with smart bidding and
       proof it works for this account.
    3. Write 7-9 RSA headlines from the brand's own offer; lead with product, price
       or offer, and let descriptions answer the real objection.
    4. Fix quality signals (landing page relevance, ad relevance) before raising a
       bid.
    5. Send cold, problem-aware clicks to an educational page, not straight to a
       buy box.
    6. Review search terms on a tighten-then-loosen cadence; promote converting
       broad terms to exact, remove clicked non-converters.
    7. Keep the account negative list clean, never blocking a real product search.

    Checks
    - No ad group mixes more than one search intent.
    - Every RSA answers an objection, not just a product description.

    Output: keyword/RSA plan, search-term cleanup log, change list.

    Example: "waterproof travel mug" search term converts well under a broad
    "travel mug" keyword -> promoted to its own exact-match keyword and ad group.

name: Performance Max control build
invoke_when: the weekly PMax control check is due, or PMax is being qualified for a new account
steps: Qualify the account before launching PMax as a conversion campaign; never launch it as the first campaign type.
Turn off final URL expansion (or restrict with URL-contains rules) and auto-created assets/automatic enhancements.
Build asset groups by product theme, 2-20 groups, never one giant group and never a single-product group.
Fill and refresh asset counts every 4-6 weeks; build the full exclusion set: brand, URL, SKU, placement, age, customer list.
Use first-party lists and proven converting search terms as signals; check for warm-traffic over-crediting before raising target ROAS.
Fix inputs in order: feed, brand exclusion, structure, bidding, signals.
Mine PMax search terms to launch dedicated Search campaigns on proven terms; test feed-only PMax to push spend toward Shopping.
Split PMax into a prospecting campaign and a remarketing/brand-defense campaign only for a real audience or goal difference.
checks: URL expansion and auto-assets are off unless a written reason keeps them on
asset groups are theme-based, never single-product
the exclusion set (brand, URL, SKU, placement, age, customer list) is complete
output: PMax control checklist + asset group plan + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-pmax
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the weekly PMax control check is due, or PMax is being qualified
    inputs: catalogue, margin, current PMax settings
    outputs: control checklist, asset group plan, change list
    ---
    Purpose: replace PMax's defaults with real controls, since the wizard's
    settings hide the levers a media buyer needs to trust the campaign.

    Steps
    1. Qualify the account first: proven feed, tracking, and existing Search/
       Shopping data. Never launch PMax as the first campaign type.
    2. Turn off final URL expansion (or restrict it) and every auto-created asset
       or automatic enhancement.
    3. Build theme-based asset groups, 2-20 of them; never one giant or single-
       product group.
    4. Build the full exclusion set: brand, URL, SKU, placement, age, customer
       list.
    5. Fix inputs in this order: feed, brand exclusion, structure, bidding,
       signals. Fixing bidding before the feed wastes the fix.
    6. Refresh asset counts every 4-6 weeks; feed proven Search terms and first-
       party lists in as signals.
    7. Check for warm-traffic over-crediting before raising target ROAS.

    Checks
    - No PMax setting is left on a default the agent has not deliberately chosen.
    - The exclusion set is complete, not partial.

    Output: control checklist, asset group plan, change list.

    Example: PMax is crediting itself for branded-search converters -> check brand
    exclusion first; it was missing, not the bidding.

name: YouTube and Demand Gen planning
invoke_when: Search and Shopping are stable, or proven Meta creative exists, and a new funnel layer is being considered
steps: Add YouTube or Demand Gen only after Search and Shopping are dialled in, or with proven Meta creative to reuse.
Check fit before spending: AOV, a visually demonstrable product, and creative/budget for 4-6 choppy weeks.
Restrict cold Demand Gen prospecting to in-stream and Shorts; other placements off. Start cold on mobile only with Meta-style vertical creative.
Never feed the store's own customer list into cold Demand Gen prospecting.
Size budget from AOV, not a flat small test amount.
Script creative to hook, then demo, then prove, then ask; use the real founder or a disclosed spokesperson in founder-style ads.
Route cold traffic to a real conversion mechanism and capture email on the page.
Judge by traffic-light KPIs at the campaign level, not gut feel per ad; wait for a steady CPA over several days before switching to target bidding.
checks: the fit checklist passed before any spend
cold Demand Gen never targets the store's own customer list
creative follows hook-demo-prove-ask
output: launch plan + creative script brief + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-youtube-demandgen
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: Search/Shopping are stable or proven Meta creative exists
    inputs: AOV, creative library, video references
    outputs: launch plan, creative script brief, change list
    ---
    Purpose: decide honestly whether the brand is ready for a video-first funnel
    layer, and if so, script and structure it so it earns a fair read.

    Steps
    1. Confirm Search and Shopping are already stable, or proven Meta creative
       exists to adapt.
    2. Check fit: AOV supports the CPM, the product demos visually, and there is
       creative and budget for 4-6 choppy early weeks.
    3. Restrict cold Demand Gen to in-stream and Shorts; keep other placements off.
    4. Size the budget from AOV, not a flat test amount.
    5. Script creative as hook, then demo, then prove, then ask.
    6. Route cold traffic to a real conversion mechanism and capture email.
    7. Judge results with traffic-light KPIs at the campaign level; hold off
       target-based bidding until CPA is steady over several days.

    Checks
    - The fit checklist passed before spend started.
    - Cold prospecting never targeted the brand's own customer list.

    Output: launch plan, creative script brief, change list.

    Example: AOV is $22 and the product cannot be demoed visually in 15
    seconds -> fit check fails; recommend against launching yet.

name: Google remarketing and exclusion lists
invoke_when: a new remarketing campaign is needed, or lists need a scheduled rebuild
inputs_required: brand brain: order history, objections list
steps: Build a cart-abandoner list from GA4 add-to-cart minus purchase.
Wait for a list to reach a usable size before launching on it.
Exclude existing customers from every prospecting campaign.
Map cart-abandonment ads to the brand's 5 real objections, not one generic reminder.
Use full-catalog dynamic remarketing for warm audiences.
Build a high-value customer list as its own lookalike seed.
checks: no list launches before it reaches a usable size
existing customers are excluded from prospecting
abandonment ads map to a real objection, not a generic nudge
skill_md:
---
    name: google-remarketing
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new remarketing campaign is needed or lists need a rebuild
    inputs: order history, GA4 events, the brand's 5 objections
    outputs: remarketing list plan, change list
    ---
    Purpose: build remarketing lists worth using, and make sure every abandonment
    ad answers a real objection instead of just repeating the offer.

    Steps
    1. Build the cart-abandoner list: GA4 add-to-cart minus purchase.
    2. Check list size against Google's usable minimum before launching.
    3. Exclude existing customers from every prospecting campaign using this data.
    4. Map each abandonment ad to one of the brand's 5 real objections.
    5. Set up full-catalog dynamic remarketing for warm audiences.
    6. Build a high-value customer list as a lookalike seed for cold.

    Checks
    - Every list that launched had reached its usable size first.
    - No abandonment ad is a generic "still thinking it over" with no objection.

    Output: remarketing list plan, change list.

    Example: cart abandoners cite shipping cost as the top exit reason -> the
    abandonment ad leads with the free-shipping threshold, not a generic discount.

name: TikTok first campaign launch
invoke_when: a new TikTok account or relaunch needs its first campaign
inputs_required: connector: none yet (manual TikTok Ads Manager)
steps: Complete the full TikTok account setup before spending any budget.
Test every pixel event before launch; stop if Purchase or Add to Cart does not fire.
Launch the first campaign as a manual Sales campaign with the catalog off.
Set the first ad group to broad targeting, Complete Payment optimisation, no target CPA.
Keep interests broad: 2-5 parent categories, never 15-20 stacked interests.
Set daily budget at the greater of $50 or 2x current CPA per ad group.
Run the first test as 2 ad groups by 3 creatives by $50/day for 3-4 days.
Read at 24 hours on soft metrics and at 3 days on cost metrics; cut the bottom half.
Pass the built campaign to `media/account-ops/trafficking-qa` before it goes live.
checks: every pixel event fires before spend starts
interests stay broad, never stacked
the 24-hour/3-day staged read actually happened before any cut
output: launch checklist + change list + first test read
skill_md:
---
    name: tiktok-launch
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new TikTok account or relaunch needs its first campaign
    inputs: catalogue, creative library, TikTok account state
    outputs: launch checklist, change list, first test read
    ---
    Purpose: get a TikTok account's first campaign live correctly, broad, and read
    on a fixed schedule, since a wrong first setup wastes the account's early data.

    Steps
    1. Complete account setup (business center, pixel, catalog connection if used)
       before any spend.
    2. Test every pixel event; stop if Purchase or Add to Cart fails to fire.
    3. Launch a manual Sales campaign, catalog off for the first test.
    4. Set the ad group to broad targeting, Complete Payment optimisation, no
       target CPA yet.
    5. Keep interests to 2-5 parent categories; never stack 15-20 interests.
    6. Set daily budget at the greater of $50 or 2x current CPA per ad group.
    7. Run 2 ad groups by 3 creatives by $50/day for 3-4 days.
    8. Read soft metrics at 24 hours, cost metrics at 3 days; cut the bottom half.
    9. Run the pre-launch QA check before anything goes live.

    Checks
    - Pixel events confirmed firing before spend.
    - No more than 5 stacked interests in any ad group.

    Output: launch checklist, change list, first test read.

    Example: Purchase event fires but with no value passed -> hold the launch,
    send a developer brief to fix value passing before spending.

name: TikTok organic-to-Spark loop and creator program
invoke_when: a creator's or the brand's organic post is ready to be tested as a paid Spark ad
steps: Post organically first; wait 5-7 days before considering Spark.
Pick the winning organic posts by early engagement, not by brand preference.
Confirm CREA-C38 has logged a 365-day authorization code for any creator post before Sparking it; if not, stop and route to CREA.
Keep hook-test variants off the public organic profile.
Structure affiliate-style commissions: open collabs for volume, targeted collabs for key partners.
Schedule the Spark push once authorization is confirmed and the post has proven organically.
checks: no creator post is Sparked without a logged, unexpired authorization code
hook-test variants stay off the public profile
skill_md:
---
    name: tiktok-spark-loop
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: an organic post is ready to be tested as a paid Spark ad
    inputs: creator relationships, CREA-C38 authorization log
    outputs: Spark loop schedule, change list
    ---
    Purpose: turn a proven organic post into a paid Spark ad without ever running
    one that lacks a valid authorization, since that is a platform violation risk.

    Steps
    1. Post organically first; give it 5-7 days before judging it for Spark.
    2. Pick winners by real early engagement, not by which post the brand likes.
    3. Check CREA-C38's authorization log for a valid, unexpired code tied to that
       exact post. If missing, stop and hand the request to CREA, do not proceed.
    4. Keep any hook-test variant off the public organic profile; only the proven
       post gets Sparked.
    5. Set commission structure: open collabs for reach, targeted collabs for the
       brand's key partners.
    6. Schedule the Spark push once authorization is confirmed.

    Checks
    - Every Sparked post has a logged, unexpired authorization code.
    - No unapproved hook variant is public.

    Output: Spark loop schedule, change list.

    Example: a creator's post is performing well on day 6, but no authorization
    code is logged -> hold the Spark request, route to CREA for the code first.

name: TikTok Shop, Search and GMV Max setup
invoke_when: TikTok Shop is launching, or the quarterly SKU review for GMV Max is due
inputs_required: brand brain: catalogue, margin by SKU
connector: none yet (manual TikTok Seller Center)
steps: Complete TikTok Shop setup in Seller Center with full listings before selling through it.
Run TikTok Search with 20-50 keywords, phrase match, and add negatives regularly.
Launch GMV Max only on the top 20 percent of SKUs by margin, with an ROI target above break-even.
Verify the TikTok Shopify app is the official one before connecting the Shop.
Test alternate Shop storefront templates against the current one.
checks: listings are complete before Shop goes live
GMV Max only touches the top 20 percent of SKUs by margin
output: TikTok Shop setup checklist + GMV Max SKU list + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: tiktok-shop-gmvmax
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: TikTok Shop is launching or the quarterly SKU review is due
    inputs: catalogue, margin by SKU, TikTok Seller Center state
    outputs: Shop setup checklist, GMV Max SKU list, change list
    ---
    Purpose: get TikTok Shop selling with complete listings, and keep GMV Max's
    automated spend limited to SKUs whose margin can absorb it.

    Steps
    1. Complete listings in Seller Center: images, descriptions, pricing, before
       any sale attempt.
    2. Verify the Shopify-TikTok connector is the official app before linking.
    3. Build TikTok Search with 20-50 keywords, phrase match; keep adding negatives.
    4. Rank SKUs by margin; put only the top 20 percent into GMV Max.
    5. Set GMV Max's ROI target above break-even for those SKUs, never a flat
       number copied from another platform.
    6. Test an alternate storefront template against the current one.

    Checks
    - No SKU with thin margin sits in GMV Max.
    - Listings are complete before any spend starts.

    Output: Shop setup checklist, GMV Max SKU list, change list.

    Example: a SKU has 18% margin while the top 20% cutoff is 35% margin -> excluded
    from GMV Max even if it is a bestseller by unit volume.

name: Amazon, Walmart and Target marketplace ad brief
invoke_when: a marketplace ad launch is coming up, or the quarterly marketplace ads review is due
inputs_required: brand's own Google Search converting terms
steps: Pull bestseller and margin data to pick which SKUs get sponsored placement first.
Propose keyword targets from the brand's own converting Google Search terms plus marketplace search suggestions.
Build the negative keyword list to exclude irrelevant marketplace searches.
Propose ACOS or TACOS targets from the SKU's actual margin, never a generic benchmark.
Propose a budget split across search, product-page and brand-store placements.
Flag catalogue or listing issues (missing bullets, weak images) that will cap performance before spend starts.
checks: ACOS/TACOS targets trace to the SKU's own margin
listing issues are flagged before spend, not after
output: marketplace ad campaign brief ready for Amazon Seller Central, Walmart Connect or Target Roundel (Flipkart Ads Manager, India only)
skill_md:
---
    name: marketplace-amazon-flipkart
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a marketplace ad launch is coming, or the quarterly review is due
    inputs: marketplace catalogue, SKU margin, converting Google Search terms
    outputs: a ready-to-execute marketplace ad brief
    ---
    Purpose: since there is no Amazon, Walmart or Target connector (or Flipkart
    connector, India only), hand a human or agency a brief complete enough to
    build the campaign correctly the first time.

    Steps
    1. Pull bestseller and margin data; rank SKUs for sponsored placement priority.
    2. Seed keyword targets from the brand's own converting Google Search terms,
       plus the marketplace's own search suggestions.
    3. Build a negative keyword list for irrelevant marketplace searches.
    4. Set ACOS or TACOS targets from each SKU's real margin, not a category
       average.
    5. Propose a budget split across search, product-page and brand-store
       placements.
    6. Check the listing itself (bullets, images, A+ content) and flag anything
       that will cap ad performance before spend starts.

    Checks
    - Every ACOS/TACOS target traces to that SKU's own margin.
    - A weak listing is flagged, not launched into ads as-is.

    Output: a full campaign brief ready to build in the marketplace's own console
    (Amazon Seller Central, Walmart Connect, Target Roundel; Flipkart Ads Manager
    for the India option).

    Example: a SKU has only 3 product images and no bullet points -> flagged to fix
    the listing before its ACOS target is set or spend begins.

name: Rapid-delivery and grocery marketplace retail media brief
invoke_when: a rapid-delivery/grocery marketplace ad push is planned, or the brand adds a new such listing (India only: a quick-commerce ad push, or a new quick-commerce listing)
inputs_required: rapid-delivery/grocery listing and stock status per fulfillment center or city (dark store, India only)
PROD-C49: per-SKU per-fulfillment-center contribution margin report (per-dark-store, India only)
steps: Check which rapid-delivery or grocery marketplace platforms (Instacart, DoorDash, Gopuff, Amazon Fresh; India only: Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart) the brand's SKUs are actually listed and in-stock on before proposing spend.
Read PROD-C49's contribution-margin report; only propose spend on a SKU with 3 consecutive weeks of positive contribution margin at that fulfillment center or dark store (India only).
Propose which SKUs to sponsor based on category search volume on that platform and current margin.
Size budget to the platform's own category CPC/ROAS benchmarks, since these differ from Meta or Google norms.
Flag stockout risk before scaling; rapid-delivery ad delivery can outpace local fulfillment-center inventory (dark-store inventory, India only).
Keep rapid-delivery/grocery marketplace ad results separate from Meta/Google reporting; attribution windows and intent differ.
checks: no SKU is sponsored without a positive contribution-margin run from PROD-C49
stockout risk is flagged before any scale-up
output: a retail media brief per platform ready for a human to execute in the platform's brand console
skill_md:
---
    name: marketplace-quick-commerce
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a rapid-delivery/grocery marketplace ad push is planned or a new listing is added (India only: a quick-commerce ad push)
    inputs: listing/stock status per fulfillment center (dark store, India only), category benchmarks, PROD-C49 margin report
    outputs: a retail media brief per platform
    ---
    Purpose: brief rapid-delivery and grocery marketplace ads (Instacart, DoorDash,
    Gopuff, Amazon Fresh; India only: Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart) only where a SKU's
    real transaction-value economics, not the platform's inflated list-price ROAS,
    already work, and only where stock can support the delivery.

    Steps
    1. Confirm the SKU is listed and in-stock at the fulfillment centers (dark
       stores, India only) the ad would run against.
    2. Read PROD-C49's contribution-margin report; require 3 consecutive positive
       weeks at that fulfillment center or dark store before proposing spend.
    3. Pick SKUs to sponsor by category search volume and current margin.
    4. Size the budget against the platform's own category CPC/ROAS benchmark, not
       a Meta or Google number.
    5. Flag stockout risk before any scale-up; rapid-delivery ad delivery can
       outpace local inventory fast.
    6. Keep the resulting report separate from Meta/Google in reporting.

    Checks
    - No SKU with a negative or unproven contribution margin is sponsored.
    - Stockout risk is checked before, not after, a budget increase.

    Output: a platform-specific retail media brief for a human to execute.

    Example: a SKU shows positive list-price-based ROAS on the platform dashboard
    but PROD-C49's transaction-value recompute shows negative margin (India only:
    the inflated number is MRP-based) -> brief holds that SKU back until the real
    number turns positive.

name: Meta creative test sizing
invoke_when: a new Meta creative test is ready to size
steps: Size the test budget with the formula: target conversions x CPA / test days; never derive it from Meta's 50-conversions-in-7-days learning rule.
Set the kill-rule threshold at 3-5x target CPA before judging.
Match the read window to purchase cycle and volume; never read under 5 days below $50k/month spend.
Never judge or kill an ad on $1-2 of spend.
Check the ad set's planned daily budget can actually reach its read-spend threshold inside the test window.
checks: the budget formula, not Meta's learning-phase rule, sized the test
the read window is never shorter than 5 days below $50k/month spend
output: test brief with budget and read window + kill-rule sheet
skill_md:
---
    name: meta-test-sizing
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new Meta creative test is ready to size
    inputs: target CPA, purchase cycle, planned test budget
    outputs: test brief, kill-rule sheet
    ---
    Purpose: size a Meta creative test so its result can actually be trusted,
    instead of leaning on the platform's own learning-phase suggestion.

    Steps
    1. Compute the test budget: target conversions x CPA / test days, in code.
    2. Set the kill-rule threshold: 3-5x target CPA before any judgement.
    3. Set the read window to match the purchase cycle; never under 5 days below
       $50k/month spend.
    4. Confirm the planned daily budget can reach the read-spend threshold within
       that window; if not, raise the budget or extend the window before launch.
    5. Never allow a same-day or $1-2-spend kill call.

    Checks
    - The budget came from the formula, not Meta's 50-conversions rule.
    - The ad set can mathematically reach its read threshold in the window given.

    Output: a test brief (budget, read window, kill rule) for the launch.

    Example: target CPA is $20, target 15 conversions to judge, test runs 5 days ->
    budget = 15 x $20 / 5 = $60/day.

name: Google bid stage and budget pacing
invoke_when: the weekly Google bid or budget review is due
inputs_required: metric contract: cpc, roas_blended, cpa, spend, aov
steps: Cap new-account bids at break-even CPA divided by conversion rate.
Move to Maximize Conversion Value once conversions start arriving; add Target ROAS only once volume supports it, set at or slightly below actual.
Step bid targets gently; never double a budget or halve a target overnight; break a Target ROAS death spiral with an aggressive cut, not a timid one.
Size Shopping/Search launch budgets at about 3-4x AOV/day; size PMax launches at $50-100/day and at least 3x non-brand CPA.
Raise budgets in small weekly steps; cut faster than you raise.
Treat 'limited by budget' as a hint to test, not proof to raise spend.
Pool same-currency countries into one MCC-level portfolio bid strategy only where they share one real goal.
checks: every bid cap traces to break-even math, not a platform suggestion
no budget was doubled or a target halved in one step
output: bid stage plan + budget plan + pacing log
skill_md:
---
    name: google-bid-budget
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the weekly Google bid or budget review is due
    inputs: CPC, CPA, AOV, spend, current bid strategy
    outputs: bid stage plan, budget plan, pacing log
    ---
    Purpose: move Google bidding and budget forward in small, reversible steps
    tied to the brand's own break-even math, never a platform default or a big
    jump.

    Steps
    1. Cap a new account's bids at break-even CPA / conversion rate.
    2. Move to Maximize Conversion Value once conversions arrive; add Target ROAS
       only once volume supports it, set near the actual number.
    3. Size Shopping/Search launch budgets at 3-4x AOV/day; PMax at $50-100/day and
       3x non-brand CPA.
    4. Raise budgets in small weekly steps; cut faster than you raise.
    5. Treat "limited by budget" as a signal to test, not an automatic raise.
    6. Step bid targets gently; use an aggressive cut, not a timid one, to break a
       Target ROAS death spiral.

    Checks
    - No budget doubled or target halved in a single step.
    - Every cap traces to the brand's own break-even math.

    Output: bid stage plan, budget plan, pacing log.

    Example: account shows "limited by budget" on a campaign at 1.5x target ROAS ->
    treated as a signal to test a modest raise, not proof to double the budget.

name: TikTok budget sizing and targeting-ladder pacing
invoke_when: a TikTok ad group needs its budget set, or the next week of the targeting ladder is due
steps: Set daily budget at the greater of $50 or 2x current CPA per ad group.
Grow structure with budget: broad ad group first, then an interest ad group, cap at 4 ad groups.
Run a 4-week targeting ladder, adding one layer per week; run one controlled 7-day broad-vs-stacked test before dropping interests or lookalikes entirely.
Wait for a new audience to finish populating before launching on it.
checks: budget never sits below $50 or 2x CPA, whichever is greater
the ladder adds exactly one layer per week, never several at once
skill_md:
---
    name: tiktok-budget-ladder
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a TikTok ad group needs budget set, or the ladder's next week is due
    inputs: current CPA per ad group, current ladder week
    outputs: budget and ladder pacing plan
    ---
    Purpose: size TikTok budget from a fixed floor tied to CPA, and add targeting
    layers on a controlled weekly cadence instead of all at once.

    Steps
    1. Set daily budget at the greater of $50 or 2x current CPA, per ad group.
    2. Add structure only with budget growth: broad first, then one interest ad
       group, capped at 4 ad groups total.
    3. Run the 4-week targeting ladder, one new layer per week.
    4. Before dropping interests or lookalikes entirely, run one controlled 7-day
       broad-vs-stacked test rather than guessing.
    5. Wait for a new audience to finish populating before spending against it.

    Checks
    - No ad group runs under the $50/2xCPA floor.
    - No more than one new targeting layer was added in a week.

    Output: a budget and ladder pacing plan.

    Example: current CPA is $30 -> daily budget floor is $60 (2x CPA), not $50.

name: Stock-aware spend pacing
invoke_when: any surface is about to raise budget or move an ad set into scaling
steps: Check live stock before raising budget or moving an ad set into the scaling campaign.
Throttle spend on a SKU ahead of a predicted stockout.
Plan stock ahead when a product starts scaling in ads.
Run a small clearance campaign for aged or grade-C inventory.
Run a dedicated new-arrivals campaign to surface fresh SKUs early.
checks: no budget increase is proposed for a SKU projected to stock out inside the scaling read window
skill_md:
---
    name: stock-check
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: any surface is about to raise budget or scale an ad set
    inputs: live stock, days_of_stock, stockout projection
    outputs: pacing report, change list
    ---
    Purpose: never let ad spend outrun what the warehouse can actually ship, and
    catch a scaling opportunity for stock that has room to grow into.

    Steps
    1. Pull live stock and days_of_stock for every SKU in a budget-raise or
       scaling decision.
    2. Throttle spend on any SKU projected to stock out before the read window
       closes.
    3. Flag a scaling product early enough that a person can order more stock
       ahead of the ramp.
    4. Suggest a small clearance campaign for aged or grade-C inventory instead of
       leaving it to sell at full price alone.
    5. Suggest a new-arrivals campaign for fresh SKUs that have not had a fair
       chance yet.

    Checks
    - No scale-up is approved for a SKU with fewer days of stock than the read
      window needs.

    Output: pacing report, change list.

    Example: a winning ad set is about to get 2x budget but the SKU has 9 days of
    stock at current velocity and a 14-day read window -> hold the raise, flag the
    stock gap first.

name: Meta daily and weekly read, anomaly and forecast
invoke_when: the daily Meta read, the weekly read, or the spend/ROAS anomaly check is due
inputs_required: connector: meta ads read, gallery cache
steps: Pull spend, orders and revenue and blend them into MER in code.
Compute the trailing 14-day median for spend and ROAS; flag any day 50 percent or more off that median.
Name the 3 ads most responsible for a flagged day; check pixel, CAPI or feed health first before blaming bidding.
Treat daily ROAS swings under about $1,000/day as normal noise, not a signal.
Split ROAS and conversion rate by device with custom columns; be in the account daily for search-term-equivalent signals and anomalies, do product/asset work weekly.
Project month-end spend and blended MER from the trailing pace in code; flag a platform pacing to miss its budget or margin target early enough to act.
Mark any missing platform or day as unavailable, never as zero.
checks: every number in the read came from code, not model arithmetic
an anomaly flag names the 3 ads most responsible and checked tracking health first
a forecast is shown next to the actual, never in place of it
output: daily read + weekly read + daily anomaly alert + spend forecast
skill_md:
---
    name: meta-daily-weekly-read
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the daily read, weekly read, or anomaly/forecast check is due
    inputs: spend, orders, revenue, trailing 14-day history
    outputs: daily read, weekly read, anomaly alert, spend forecast
    ---
    Purpose: give the founder one page a day and one a week on what is spent, what
    it returned, what moved sharply, and where the month is headed, all computed
    in code.

    Steps
    1. Blend spend, orders and revenue into MER in code.
    2. Compute the trailing 14-day median for spend and ROAS; flag days 50%+ off
       it.
    3. On a flagged day, check pixel/CAPI/feed health before blaming bidding; name
       the 3 ads that moved most.
    4. Treat sub-$1,000/day swings as noise, not signal.
    5. Split ROAS and conversion rate by device.
    6. Project month-end spend and MER from the trailing pace; flag a miss early.
    7. Mark any missing platform or day as unavailable, never zero.

    Checks
    - Every number traces to code, never model arithmetic.
    - No computed 0 hides a genuinely missing data point.

    Output: daily read, weekly read, anomaly alert, spend forecast.

    Example: ROAS drops 60% against the 14-day median on a Tuesday -> check CAPI
    health first; a dropped event, not bidding, explains the drop.

name: TikTok staged and ladder reads
invoke_when: a TikTok test's 24-hour or 3-day read point is due, or a targeting-ladder week needs reading
steps: Read soft metrics (CTR, video views, add-to-cart) at 24 hours; read cost metrics (CPA, ROAS) at 3 days.
Cut the bottom half of ad groups or creatives at the 3-day read, never before.
Read a targeting-ladder week's result before deciding whether to add the next layer.
Read placement performance after a fixed period before opting weak automatic placements out.
checks: no cut happens before its scheduled read point
soft metrics are never used alone to make a cost decision
skill_md:
---
    name: tiktok-staged-read
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a 24-hour/3-day read point or ladder week is due
    inputs: ad group metrics, the test's read schedule
    outputs: staged test read, ladder-week read
    ---
    Purpose: read TikTok tests on the schedule that actually produces a trustworthy
    signal, since TikTok's own data can look decisive before it is.

    Steps
    1. At 24 hours, read soft metrics only: CTR, video views, add-to-cart rate.
    2. At 3 days, read cost metrics: CPA, ROAS; only now cut the bottom half.
    3. For a targeting-ladder week, read that week's isolated result before adding
       the next layer.
    4. After a fixed placement-read period, decide which automatic placements to
       opt out, not before.

    Checks
    - No ad group was cut before its 3-day cost read.
    - A ladder layer was judged on its own week's data, not blended with prior
      weeks.

    Output: a staged test read, a ladder-week read.

    Example: at 24 hours one ad group has a weak CTR but decent add-to-cart -> held
    to the 3-day cost read rather than cut early on CTR alone.

name: Marketplace and rapid-delivery/grocery marketplace read
invoke_when: a marketplace or rapid-delivery/grocery marketplace spend read is due (India only: a quick-commerce spend read)
inputs_required: rapid-delivery/grocery seller dashboard export (quick-commerce, India only)
Amazon/Walmart/Target ad console export (Flipkart, India only)
steps: Recompute ROAS on actual transaction value, not list price, net of platform commission (15-25%) and applicable US sales tax on commission (GST, India only).
Track inwarding fees, storage cost and damage/expiry write-off (budgeted 2-5% of list price) per SKU.
Calculate weekly per-fulfillment-center order volume needed to clear the 55-60% gross margin floor (per-dark-store, India only).
Flag whether a margin problem is volume (fixable with more orders) or structural (needs repricing or a COGS cut).
Read Amazon/Walmart/Target ACOS or TACOS against the SKU's real margin, not the platform's own benchmark (Flipkart, India only).
checks: ROAS is read on transaction value, never on the platform's list-price-based number (MRP-based, India only)
every margin flag says whether it is a volume problem or a structural one
output: per-SKU per-fulfillment-center contribution margin report + ACOS/TACOS read (per-dark-store, India only)
skill_md:
---
    name: marketplace-read
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a marketplace or rapid-delivery/grocery spend read is due (India only: quick-commerce)
    inputs: seller dashboard export, SKU landed cost, ad console export
    outputs: contribution margin report, ACOS/TACOS read
    ---
    Purpose: read marketplace and rapid-delivery/grocery ad results on the real
    number, since platform dashboards inflate ROAS 30-50% by pricing at list price
    (MRP, India) instead of transaction value.

    Steps
    1. Recompute ROAS on actual transaction value, net of platform commission
       (15-25%) and applicable US sales tax on the commission (GST, India only).
    2. Add inwarding fees, storage cost and a 2-5% list-price write-off budget for
       damage/expiry.
    3. Calculate the weekly per-fulfillment-center order volume needed to clear the
       55-60% gross margin floor (per-dark-store, India only).
    4. Flag whether a shortfall is a volume problem (more orders fixes it) or a
       structural one (needs repricing or a COGS cut).
    5. Read Amazon/Walmart/Target ACOS or TACOS against the SKU's own margin
       (Flipkart, India only).

    Checks
    - No ROAS number in the report is based on list price (MRP, India only).
    - Every margin flag names whether it is volume or structural.

    Output: contribution margin report, ACOS/TACOS read.

    Example: platform dashboard shows 4.2x ROAS; recomputed on transaction value
    net of commission and fees it is 2.6x -> the true number the SKU is judged on.

name: Meta ad set kill, keep or scale
invoke_when: the daily Meta read produced ad-set-level numbers that need a call
steps: Apply the keep/yellow/kill table read at 3-5x target CPA, at the ad-set level, never on one ad's own ROAS.
Never touch a winning ad set directly; fork new creative into a new ad set beside it.
Never run creative tests inside the scaling campaign.
Rescue a high-conviction, CBO-starved ad in a small, separate, capped and logged ad set.
Raise a winning ad set's budget in steps sized to the read window, never a fixed percentage; find its spend equilibrium by stepping up until ROAS turns unprofitable, then pull back.
Move only confirmed equilibrium winners into a dedicated scaling campaign.
Judge every budget raise over 7+ days, never on same-day revenue; confirm a winner acquires new customers under 7-day click before briefing more of it.
Flag high frequency on a top-spending prospecting ad before scaling it further.
checks: the call was made at the ad-set level, never on one ad
a winner was forked or stepped, never edited directly
a scale-up was read over 7+ days before being confirmed
output: daily read with keep/kill/scale calls + change list for budget moves
skill_md:
---
    name: meta-kill-scale
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: daily ad-set metrics need a keep, kill or scale call
    inputs: CPA, ROAS, frequency at ad-set level
    outputs: daily call list, change list for budget moves
    ---
    Purpose: make Meta's daily budget calls a fixed table read, and scale a winner
    by finding its real spend equilibrium instead of riding it blind.

    Steps
    1. Read the keep/yellow/kill table at 3-5x target CPA, at the ad-set level.
    2. Never touch a winning ad set directly; fork new creative beside it instead.
    3. Keep creative tests out of the scaling campaign entirely.
    4. For a high-conviction ad starved by CBO, rescue it in a small, capped,
       logged ad set of its own.
    5. Step a winner's budget up in sizes matched to the read window; find the
       point ROAS turns unprofitable, then pull back to just before it.
    6. Move only a confirmed equilibrium winner into the dedicated scaling
       campaign.
    7. Judge any raise over 7+ days; confirm new-customer share under 7-day click
       before briefing more of that creative.
    8. Flag rising frequency on a top-spending prospecting ad before scaling it.

    Checks
    - No call was made on one ad's number inside a larger ad set.
    - No winner was edited in place; it was forked or stepped.

    Output: daily call list, change list.

    Example: an ad set holds at 3.8x target CPA for 8 days after a 20% budget
    step -> equilibrium found; hold there, do not step again this week.

name: Google scaling gate check
invoke_when: a budget increase or new campaign type is being considered for Google
steps: Pass the 5 fixed scaling gates before adding budget or a new campaign type.
Scale only a campaign that already hits target ROAS at its current budget.
Cut fast in steady state, but scale fast on a clear winner or a real demand spike.
Scale YouTube in order: more budget and creative first, then better hooks and offers, then new formats.
checks: all 5 gates passed before any increase is approved
no campaign scales before it proves target ROAS at current spend
output: scaling gate checklist result + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: google-scaling-gates
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a Google budget increase or new campaign type is proposed
    inputs: ROAS, spend, the account's 5 scaling gates
    outputs: scaling gate checklist result, change list
    ---
    Purpose: earn a Google budget increase through 5 fixed gates instead of a gut
    call, while still moving fast on a genuine winner.

    Steps
    1. Check the campaign already hits target ROAS at its current budget; if not,
       stop here.
    2. Run the 5 scaling gates in order and record a pass/fail on each.
    3. In steady state, cut underperformance fast; do not wait out a slow bleed.
    4. On a clear winner or a real demand spike, move fast rather than the usual
       small weekly step.
    5. For YouTube, scale in order: budget and creative first, then hooks and
       offers, then new formats.

    Checks
    - Every gate has a recorded pass/fail, not a summary judgement.
    - No increase went through with a failed gate unaddressed.

    Output: scaling gate checklist result, change list.

    Example: a campaign hits target ROAS but fails the frequency-of-conversion
    gate -> hold the budget increase until that gate passes.

name: TikTok scale winners and cut losers
invoke_when: a TikTok test's 3-day read is in, or a targeting-ladder week's result is in
steps: Cut the bottom half of ad groups or creatives at the 3-day read.
Move a winning creative into its own CBO scaling campaign, while testing continues in the manual campaign.
Opt weak automatic placements out after a placement read.
Drop a targeting-ladder layer that did not earn its week before adding the next one; run one controlled 7-day broad-vs-stack test before dropping interests or lookalikes entirely.
checks: a winner moves to its own scaling campaign, testing never stops in the manual campaign
no ladder layer survives past its proving week without a result
output: scaling plan + kill list + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: tiktok-kill-scale
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a 3-day read or ladder week's result is in
    inputs: ad group metrics, the staged or ladder read
    outputs: scaling plan, kill list, change list
    ---
    Purpose: move a proven TikTok creative into a real scaling campaign while
    keeping the testing lane alive, and prune weak layers before they compound.

    Steps
    1. Cut the bottom half of ad groups/creatives at the 3-day cost read.
    2. Move a winner into its own CBO scaling campaign; keep testing running in the
       manual campaign in parallel.
    3. Opt out weak automatic placements after a placement read.
    4. Drop a targeting-ladder layer that did not earn its proving week before
       adding another.
    5. Run one controlled 7-day broad-vs-stack test before abandoning interests or
       lookalikes for good.

    Checks
    - Testing continued in the manual campaign even after a winner moved to
      scaling.
    - No ladder layer was kept past its proving week without a positive result.

    Output: scaling plan, kill list, change list.

    Example: a hook wins its 3-day read at 2.1x target CPA -> moved to its own CBO
    scaling campaign; the manual campaign keeps testing the next 3 hooks.

name: Marketplace SKU hold, scale or kill
invoke_when: a quick-commerce or marketplace SKU's margin read is in
inputs_required: PROD-C49: per-SKU per-dark-store contribution margin report
steps: Hold expansion to new SKUs or cities until 3 consecutive weeks of positive contribution margin.
Scale a SKU only where margin is positive and stock supports the ramp.
Kill or de-prioritise a SKU whose margin problem is structural (repricing or COGS), not volume.
Pull a marketplace ad when stockout risk from `media/pace-budget/stock-check` outruns the read window.
checks: no SKU scales without 3 consecutive positive-margin weeks
a structural margin problem is never treated as a volume problem
skill_md:
---
    name: marketplace-kill-scale
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a quick-commerce or marketplace SKU's margin read is in
    inputs: PROD-C49 contribution margin report, stockout risk
    outputs: scale/hold/kill recommendation per SKU
    ---
    Purpose: scale a marketplace or quick-commerce SKU only once its real,
    transaction-value margin has proven positive for long enough to trust, and
    stop confusing a fixable volume problem with a structural one.

    Steps
    1. Read PROD-C49's per-SKU per-dark-store contribution margin.
    2. Hold any new SKU or city expansion until 3 consecutive positive-margin
       weeks.
    3. For a SKU below the margin floor, check whether more orders would clear it
       (volume) or whether price/cost is the real problem (structural).
    4. Kill or de-prioritise a structural loser rather than keep testing volume
       fixes on it.
    5. Check stockout risk before approving any scale-up.

    Checks
    - No scale-up happened before 3 consecutive positive weeks.
    - No structural loser was left running on the theory that more orders will
      fix it.

    Output: a scale/hold/kill recommendation per SKU.

    Example: a SKU has been margin-negative for 5 weeks despite rising order
    volume -> flagged structural (COGS or price), recommended for repricing or
    kill, not further ad spend.

name: Meta account audit
invoke_when: the monthly Meta audit is due
inputs_required: connector: meta ads read (gallery cache + MCP re-pull)
steps: Pull account, campaign, ad set and ad level data for the trailing 12 months from the gallery cache and a fresh Meta re-pull.
Run the structure review checklist: campaign purpose lines, ad set count vs spend tier, naming, CBO vs ABO use.
Run the creative review in fixed order: volume, then diversity, then quality.
Score the account on a readable-data test and a commercial-alignment test.
Validate any proposed structure change against 4 fixed questions before it goes in the roadmap.
Rank findings by money at stake, not by how easy they are to fix.
Write the roadmap as dated, ranked actions with the metric each one should move.
checks: the roadmap names one biggest constraint, not ten equal findings
every finding has a number and a source
output: audit report + ranked 90-day roadmap + change list for structure fixes
skill_md:
---
    name: audit-meta
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the monthly Meta account audit is due
    inputs: 12 months of account/campaign/ad-set/ad data
    outputs: audit report, ranked 90-day roadmap, change list
    ---
    Purpose: turn a raw Meta account into one ranked constraint a founder can act
    on, not a list of screenshots or ten equal-weight observations.

    Steps
    1. Pull 12 months of account, campaign, ad set and ad data from the gallery
       cache plus a fresh re-pull.
    2. Run the structure checklist: purpose lines, ad-set count vs spend tier,
       naming, CBO/ABO use.
    3. Run the creative review in order: volume, then diversity, then quality.
    4. Score the account on readable-data and commercial-alignment tests.
    5. Validate any structure change idea against 4 fixed questions before it
       enters the roadmap.
    6. Rank every finding by money at stake, not ease of fix.
    7. Write the roadmap as dated, ranked actions, each with the metric it should
       move.

    Checks
    - The roadmap names ONE biggest constraint, not a flat list.
    - Every finding has a number and a source.

    Output: audit report, ranked 90-day roadmap, change list.

    Example: naming is inconsistent AND creative volume is thin -> roadmap ranks
    creative volume first because it is costing more, names naming as a fast,
    smaller fix underneath it.

name: Google Ads account audit and diagnosis
invoke_when: the monthly Google Ads audit is due
steps: Pull account and campaign structure, spend and conversions (manual export).
Diagnose any dip top down: business level, then channel share, then campaign, then metric, then root cause.
Apply the 3 pre-diagnosis rules before touching any setting.
Find the inflection date of a change and check only the top 5 campaigns by spend around it.
Match the failure-mode checklist to the campaign type that dipped (Search, Shopping, PMax, Demand Gen).
Split CPA and clicks into their formula parts (impressions, CTR, CVR) to find the real cause.
Default to an isolated fix over a full rebuild unless the isolated fix has already failed.
checks: the diagnosis followed the order the problem actually happened, not a guess
an isolated fix was tried before any rebuild was proposed
output: audit report + diagnosis writeup with root cause + change list
skill_md:
---
    name: audit-google
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the monthly Google Ads audit is due
    inputs: account/campaign structure, spend, conversions
    outputs: audit report, diagnosis writeup, change list
    ---
    Purpose: diagnose a Google account top down, in the order a problem actually
    unfolds, instead of jumping straight to a setting change.

    Steps
    1. Pull account and campaign structure, spend and conversions.
    2. Diagnose top down: business level, then channel share, then campaign, then
       metric, then root cause.
    3. Apply the 3 pre-diagnosis rules before touching anything.
    4. Find the inflection date of any dip; check only the top 5 campaigns by
       spend around that date.
    5. Match the failure-mode checklist to the campaign type that dipped.
    6. Split CPA and clicks into impressions, CTR and CVR to isolate the real
       cause.
    7. Try the isolated fix first; propose a rebuild only after it has failed.

    Checks
    - The diagnosis order was followed, not skipped to a favorite fix.
    - An isolated fix was tried before any rebuild reached the roadmap.

    Output: audit report, diagnosis writeup with root cause, change list.

    Example: CPA rose 30% -> traced to a CTR drop, not a CVR drop -> points to an
    ad-fatigue or ranking cause, not a landing-page cause.

name: Account access, ownership and multi-account scaling
invoke_when: the quarterly access review is due
steps: Confirm the ad account, Merchant Center and analytics sit under one master login.
Lock down Business Center access before adding any team member.
Check whether a second ad account on the same pixel is justified (only once spend passes about $250k/month).
Confirm ad accounts are not split by country except to bill in local currency.
Audit who has admin, employee or partner access on every connected account.
checks: no account is split by country without a currency reason
a second account is not opened below the $250k/month threshold
skill_md:
---
    name: access-audit
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the quarterly access review is due
    inputs: account inventory, current access list
    outputs: access audit, change list
    ---
    Purpose: keep account ownership simple and access locked down before it
    becomes an operational risk or a growth blocker.

    Steps
    1. Confirm the ad account, Merchant Center and analytics sit under one master
       login.
    2. Lock down Business Center access before any new team member joins.
    3. Check the $250k/month spend threshold before approving a second ad account
       on the same pixel.
    4. Confirm accounts are not split by country without a currency reason.
    5. List every admin, employee and partner on every connected account.

    Checks
    - No account split exists without a stated currency reason.
    - No second account was opened under the spend threshold.

    Output: access audit, change list.

    Example: spend just crossed $260k/month and checkout in a second currency is
    needed -> a second ad account is now justified; propose it with a reason.

name: Cross-border and multi-market ad delivery setup
invoke_when: a new market launch is planned
inputs_required: brand brain: markets served, shipping policy
connector: meta ads read, google merchant center (manual)
steps: Give cross-border buyers their own currency, delivery time and duty messaging in ad copy.
Set local payment methods, language and currency defaults for a mobile-first, non-US market.
Show shipping cost and import duty in the Google feed for cross-border orders.
Run one Google feed per currency.
checks: every new market has its own currency, duty and delivery-time messaging
no feed mixes two currencies
skill_md:
---
    name: cross-border-setup
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new market launch is planned
    inputs: markets served, shipping policy
    outputs: market setup checklist, change list
    ---
    Purpose: set every new market up with its own honest currency, duty and
    delivery message before ads run there, since a wrong promise on delivery time
    or landed cost creates the exact objection the ad should be preventing.

    Steps
    1. Set local currency, payment methods and language defaults for the new,
       mobile-first, non-US market.
    2. Write duty and delivery-time messaging specific to that market into the ad
       copy.
    3. Show shipping cost and import duty in the Google feed for cross-border
       orders.
    4. Run one Google feed per currency; never mix currencies in one feed.

    Checks
    - Every market's ads state its own delivery time and duty, not a generic one.
    - No feed mixes currencies.

    Output: market setup checklist, change list.

    Example: launching into Canada from a US-based store -> new feed in CAD,
    duty and delivery time called out in ad copy, separate from the US feed.

name: Peak sale ramp and wind-down plan
invoke_when: a known sale is 3-4 weeks out
inputs_required: brand brain: sale calendar, stock levels
steps: Set the ramp schedule: budget steps, new creative, and structure changes before the sale window.
Fix a wind-down date and budget step-down before the sale starts, not during it.
Prepare Google Shopping, Search and brand campaigns for the known sale date in advance.
Check stock levels against the planned ramp before committing budget.
Write the post-sale review checklist and read point.

---
# Reconcile a settlement source

## Purpose
Every outside source (a gateway, a marketplace, a card network dispute, an ad platform, or for an India-selling brand a COD courier) pays, bills or reverses money on its own schedule and its own math. This skill is the dispatcher: it picks the right sub-skill by source and never lets a gap get filed away as rounding.

## Steps
1. Pull the source's statement for the period.
2. Match `select_by.source` to gateway, marketplace, ad-platform-invoices, chargebacks, or cod-courier (India option) and hand off to that child skill.
3. Run `money.reconciliation` with the source's own unbundling rule (fee, commission, facilitator sales tax or GST/TCS on fee, refund, shipping fee as separate lines).
4. Match the unbundled total to the actual bank credit or the actual ad spend logged.
5. Name a cause for every gap over a small tolerance.
6. Draft the journal entry from the unbundled lines, one entry per settlement.

## Checks
- No gap is left unexplained.
- Facilitator sales tax (or TCS and GST for India) on fees are always their own lines.
- The matched total ties to a real bank credit, not an assumption.

## Output
A reconciliation table with source, period, matched total, gap total, named gap causes and draft journal entries.

## Example
A Meta invoice of $4,230 for the month is matched against $4,185 logged in the spend dashboard. The $45 gap is named: a late-arriving credit from the prior invoice, not rounding.

---
# Reconcile payment gateway settlement

## Purpose
A gateway payout is never the same as gross sales. This skill unbundles every payout into its real parts so the books never show one lump deposit.

## Steps
1. Pull the settlement file for the period and the matching bank statement.
2. For each payout, unbundle gross sale, gateway fee, refund, sales tax charged on the fee (GST on the fee for India-selling brands), and any FX adjustment for cross-border payments.
3. Match the net figure to the actual bank credit.
4. Age any payout not credited inside the gateway's stated settlement window (typically T+1 to T+3).
5. Draft the journal entry with each unbundled line as its own account.

## Checks
- Fee and tax on fee never merge into one line.
- FX adjustment is separated from the fee, never hidden inside it.
- An aged payout carries a day count, not a vague 'pending' label.

## Output
One row per payout: gross, fee, tax on fee, refund, FX adjustment, net, bank match status, age in days.

## Example
A Stripe payout of $1,180 unbundles to $1,225 gross sale, minus $21 fee, minus $4 tax on the fee, minus $20 refunds, net $1,180, matched to the bank credit dated 2 days later.

# Reconcile marketplace settlement

## Purpose
Marketplace settlements bury commission, fees, facilitator sales tax and refunds inside one payout figure. This skill pulls them apart and checks the marketplace charged what it agreed to.

## Steps
1. Pull the settlement report and the marketplace's 1099-K or facilitator tax statement for the period (TCS certificate for India-selling brands).
2. Unbundle commission, fixed fee, shipping fee, marketplace-facilitator sales tax withheld, and refunds (TCS under Section 52 and GST on fees, for India).
3. Match facilitator sales tax withheld (or TCS deducted, for India) in the settlement to the marketplace's own statement or certificate.
4. Match every refund line in the settlement to an actual return in the order data.
5. Check the commission rate charged against the brand's agreed rate card by category.
6. Flag any mismatch with the exact order or SKU it came from.

## Checks
- Facilitator sales tax (or TCS for India) is never assumed correct; it is matched to the marketplace's own statement.
- A refund with no matching return is flagged, not silently accepted.
- The commission rate check is per category, since rates vary by category.

## Output
One row per payout with gross, commission, fixed fee, shipping fee, facilitator tax, refunds, net and a rate-card check result.

## Example
An Amazon payout shows 15 percent commission on a category the rate card sets at 12.5 percent; the 2.5 point gap is flagged against the specific SKU category before the settlement is booked.

---
# Reconcile COD cash and courier remittance

## Purpose
COD cash sits with the courier until it is remitted. This skill ages that gap by courier so a slow remittance is caught before it becomes a cash problem instead of an accounting afterthought.

## Steps
1. Pull the courier's own collection report and remittance report for the period.
2. Match collected cash per order to the remittance that eventually lands in the bank.
3. Age every gap in days, by courier, against that courier's own stated SLA cycle.
4. For any remittance stuck past the SLA, build the escalation note: the order IDs, the amount, and the SLA clause it breaches.
5. Feed the unremitted total into the cash forecast as a receivable, never as cash in hand.

## Checks
- Aging never blends couriers together; each courier has its own SLA cycle.
- An escalation cites the SLA clause by name, not a general complaint.
- Unremitted COD lowers the cash forecast's available cash, it does not inflate it.

## Output
A table by courier: collected, remitted, gap, age in days, SLA cycle days, and an escalation flag with order IDs where the gap exceeds the SLA.

## Example
Courier X's SLA is a 7-day remittance cycle; an 82,000 rupee batch sits at 11 days. The escalation names the 34 order IDs and cites the 7-day clause in the courier's own service agreement.

## Market note
This skill applies only to an India-selling brand that runs cash on delivery. It reads null for a US-only brand, whose payout reconciliation runs through money/reconcile/gateway and money/reconcile/marketplace, with money/reconcile/chargebacks handling disputes.

---
# Reconcile ad platform invoices to logged spend

## Purpose
Ad platforms bill on their own cycle, which rarely lines up cleanly with a calendar month or with the currency the dashboard reports in. This skill catches the gap before it distorts the P&L's marketing cost line.

## Steps
1. Pull the platform's invoice for the billing period.
2. Pull the dashboard's logged spend for the matching period, as a period total, never an average of daily figures.
3. Compare the two totals directly.
4. If they differ, check for a billing-cycle boundary mismatch, a currency conversion difference, or a credit or refund applied by the platform.
5. Name the exact cause; never file the gap as unexplained variance.

## Checks
- Comparison always uses period totals, never daily averages.
- A currency conversion gap states the rate used on each side.
- The gap becomes a line in the platform-to-books reconciliation, not a silent write-off.

## Output
One line per platform per period: invoiced amount, logged amount, gap, and the named cause.

## Example
Meta's invoice covers the 3rd to the 2nd of the next month, while the dashboard reports calendar months; the resulting $620 shift is named as a billing-cycle boundary, not a spend discrepancy.

# Reconcile and represent chargebacks and disputes

## Purpose
A chargeback or dispute is a reversal, not a return: it goes through the card network or PayPal, on their own deadline, and needs its own evidence packet. This skill treats it as a first-class reconciliation source, the same as a gateway or marketplace payout, and never lets a filing deadline slip.

## Steps
1. Pull every open dispute from each gateway or processor (Shopify Payments, Stripe, PayPal), with its reason code, amount and deadline.
2. Assemble the evidence packet the specific reason code calls for: proof of delivery, customer communication, IP/device match, policy acceptance.
3. File representment before the deadline.
4. Track whether the representment won or lost, and log the reason code either way.
5. Roll the result into the win-rate report by reason code and gateway.

## Checks
- No dispute is missing a filing deadline.
- The evidence packet is built for the specific reason code, not a one-size packet.
- Win rate is tracked by reason code and gateway, never blended into one number.

## Output
One row per dispute: gateway, reason code, amount, deadline, evidence packet, and outcome once resolved.

## Example
A Stripe dispute with reason code 'product not received' gets a packet built from the shipping carrier's delivery confirmation and the customer's own delivery-confirmation email, filed two days before the ten-day deadline.

## Market note
An India-selling brand runs the same skill for a UPI dispute, assembling the OTP log alongside delivery proof and support chat.

# Build and monitor the 13-week cash forecast

## Purpose
Find the lowest cash point before it happens, and never let an inventory plan assume cash that will not be there.

## Steps
1. Pull bank balance, payroll calendar, ad spend plan, inventory on order and supplier lead times.
2. Build the rolling 13-week forecast week by week.
3. Reconcile this month's profit to free cash flow and check the 4 known cash traps (inventory build, tax timing, prepaid deposits, return timing).
4. Flag the lowest projected week at least 3 weeks ahead, with a sensitivity range.
5. Roll inventory forward against supplier lead time, targeting days-of-inventory to that lead time.

## Checks
- Inventory is never modeled to go negative.

- The lowest point is flagged with enough lead time to act.

## Output
The 13-week table, the lowest-cash-week flag with sensitivity, the inventory cash plan and the cash conversion cycle.

Week 9 is flagged as the lowest point due to a supplier deposit and a state sales-tax payment landing the same week; the flag fires in week 5, giving 4 weeks to arrange a bridge.

## Checks
- A vendor's accuracy claim is never repeated as fact; it is labeled as a vendor claim to verify.
- The recommendation states the real cost against the brand's own current accuracy, not against a competitor's case study.

## Output
Tool name, cost, claimed accuracy gain, the brand's own current accuracy, and a recommendation.

A tool costing 2,400 dollars a month claims a 15 percent accuracy gain; the brand's own recent holdout tests already track within 8 percent of platform-reported ROAS, so the recommendation is park until the gap widens.

# Track US sales tax nexus and filing compliance (GST/HSN for India)

## Purpose
Track the mechanics that feed a state sales-tax filing (a GST filing for India-selling brands) so the brand's own accountant or filing service files correctly and on time; this skill tracks, it does not file.

## Steps
1. Build the SKU-to-product-tax-code map in Avalara or TaxJar and validate every category match (SKU-to-HSN/SAC map for India, where a wrong or short code is a common cause of e-invoice portal rejections).
2. Track sales-tax nexus and registration thresholds per state the brand sells into.
3. Prepare the return-ready sales and exemption data each state's filing needs (GSTR-1 and 3B inputs matched against GSTR-2B, for India).
4. Reconcile marketplace-facilitator sales tax and 1099-K totals against the credit or exclusion actually available (TCS collected under Section 52 and TDS deducted, for India).
5. India only: raise e-way bills for B2B dispatch and stock transfer above the threshold.
6. Check that every completed return or refund has a matching sales-tax credit memo issued and filed on time (a GST credit note, for India).

## Checks
- No SKU ships without a validated tax code.
- Facilitator sales tax (or TCS and GST on fees, for India) are always separate lines.
- A refund without a matching credit memo is flagged before the filing period closes.

## Output
The requested scope's result: tax-code map, nexus status, filing input pack, facilitator-credit reconciliation, credit-memo reconciliation, or (India only) e-way bill log.

## Example
A new SKU crosses economic nexus in a state before its first sale there is registered; the nexus tracker flags the state before the next filing deadline, avoiding an unregistered-collection gap.

## Market note
An India-selling brand runs the HSN/SAC, e-way bill and GSTR path instead, which reads null for a US-only brand.

# Run the weekly fraud, bot and abuse scan

## Purpose
Catch card-testing, bot traffic, return abuse and domain impersonation early, with friction placed at checkout and account changes, never at ordinary browsing.

## Steps
1. Rebuild the bot and AI-agent traffic baseline by agent, endpoint and intent, and re-score risk tiers continuously.
2. Check for card-testing bursts (clusters of small failed authorizations) and review AVS/CVV/3DS settings against the false-decline rate.
3. Set the chargeback alert threshold below the processor's own flag level, and set step-up verification triggers for repeat abuse (prepayment triggers for repeat COD refusers, for India-selling brands).
4. Detect return and refund abuse: wardrobing, serial high-return customers, refunds without a matching return.
5. Watch the domain registrar lock status, DNS for dangling records, and lookalike domains or counterfeit listings.

## Checks
- No rule relies on User-Agent alone.
- Fraud caught is always tracked alongside the false-decline rate.

## Output
The traffic baseline, fraud and return-abuse flags, the domain watch result, and a ranked weekly fix list.

## Example
A burst of 40 small authorizations under $1 each from the same IP range is flagged as card-testing before any of them succeed at a full-value order.

Confirm the controls that stop an account takeover or a site defect from becoming a real incident, and prove a backup actually restores.

## Steps

- A restore test actually opens a restored file; it is not just a scheduled job that ran.

The auth audit, the web-app defect list with a developer fix list, the backup and restore test result, and the updated runbook.

## Example
A scheduled backup has run every night for 6 months but the restore test this month fails silently on a corrupted archive; the audit catches it before an actual incident would have.

## Purpose
Run the recurring program with a named owner per pillar, so nothing waits for an incident to get checked.

A single system's own alert stays quiet when a login looks normal to it; this skill compares the same person's logins across every admin-level system at once.
