# Organic channel and platform strategy

## Purpose
Decide which platforms a brand organically runs, with a reason tied to the avatar and a fixed test window for anything new, not a copy of what competitors do.

## Steps
1. Read the avatar, category, region and voice from the brand brain, including whether Spanish or another language outperforms English captions for this audience, and the mobile-only browsing share. India only (markets IN, reads null for a US-only brand): note whether the avatar buys on WhatsApp, and whether Hindi or a regional language outperforms English captions.
2. Pull the competitive teardown for structure and cadence only, never text or footage.
3. Score each platform: avatar fit, cost to produce one week of content, a 2-week trial success bar.
4. Set 3-5 content pillars, each naming a SKU and the objection it answers.
5. Lock the visual world (palette, type, caption style) so every account reads as one brand.
6. Write the account setup checklist and a platform-policy compliance check.
7. Package as a plain-English card for the founder to approve any new account, platform drop, or account-type change.

- Every pillar names a SKU and an objection.
- No platform runs past its trial date without a founder decision.
- Visual spec matches approved brand assets.

## Output
{positioning_brief, platform_plan[], visual_world_spec, account_setup_checklist}

## Example
Pillar "Why it does not wobble on potholed US streets" ties to the SKU "stroller-v2" and the objection "will it survive potholes", scheduled 2x a week on Instagram and YouTube Shorts only, with Pinterest on a 2-week trial ending 15 Oct.

Turn owned conversation into a report Product and Operations can act on, separate from social listening's outward-facing trend digest, and catch a spike in one theme against a real prior number.

## Steps
1. Pull comments, DMs, reviews and community-space conversations for the period.
2. Cluster into themes (a defect, a sizing issue, a delivery complaint, a feature request), each with a quote and a count.
3. Compare each theme's volume against the prior report to catch a real spike.
4. Split content-relevant feedback from operational feedback; route operational themes to Product and Operations, not just into a content idea pile.
5. Write the report with quoted evidence per theme and its routing.

## Checks
- Every theme has a quote and a count.
- A spike claim compares to the prior period's real number.
- Operational themes are actually routed, not left unaddressed.

## Output
{themes[]}

## Example
"Zipper stuck after 2 weeks" appears 14 times this month vs 3 last month, a 4.7x jump, routed to Product with 5 verbatim quotes attached.

# SEO and AEO roadmap and prioritization

## Purpose
Decide whether SEO/AEO is worth the spend at all before sequencing any work, since organic work is slow and can be wasted on a low-demand or thin-margin category.

## Steps
1. Check category demand trend and per-SKU margin first; a category failing either does not get recommended spend.
2. Sequence work: technical floor first, then money pages, then one content cluster at a time, then AEO.
3. Filter the idea bank by the brand's current bottleneck and store tags to fill each stage with ranked candidates.
4. Write an expectation memo stating a realistic timeline in months, not weeks, so the founder does not compare it to paid media's speed.
5. Package as a founder-gate card, running a founder-question round on anything the data cannot settle.

## Checks
- No content-cluster work proposed before the technical floor passes.
- Every recommendation ties to a demand or margin number.
- Timeline expectation is realistic, not inflated.

## Output
{roadmap{}, expectation_memo, open_questions[]}

## Example
Category "premium baby strollers" shows rising search volume and healthy margin: roadmap opens with the technical floor fix, then the stroller-v2 product page, before any blog cluster.

# Technical SEO and AI-crawlability audit

## Purpose
Find and prioritize the technical floor a site needs before any content work matters: indexing, canonicals, sitemap, robots.txt, redirects, heading structure, and whether AI crawlers can even read the site, while handing anything speed-related to the Site specialist rather than re-doing that work here.

## Steps
1. Crawl the whole site with mobile and JS rendering for indexing, canonical, sitemap, robots and heading-structure problems.
2. Check AI-bot access explicitly (GPTBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended) against robots.txt and CDN bot rules; this is not covered by a classic crawl.
3. Log a speed baseline from the existing instrument without diagnosing or fixing it here.
4. Order findings with the technical floor first.
5. Attach verifiable evidence to every finding: URL, response code, screenshot or quoted setting.
6. Split findings into ones this agent can brief directly and speed items that go to Site with a developer-brief hand-off note.
7. Package the prioritized fix list and hand-off note.

## Checks
- Every finding has verifiable evidence.
- AI-crawler access checked explicitly.
- Speed items only handed off, never fixed here.

## Output
{fix_list[], ai_crawler_access_report, speed_handoff_note}

## Example
Finding: "12 product pages return a soft-404 with 200 status", evidence: 12 URLs with screenshot, priority: technical floor, fixed by a canonical/redirect brief; a slow LCP finding is handed to Site instead of diagnosed further here.

# Screen a candidate

## Purpose
Kill a weak candidate before a single hour of deep research is spent on it. This is the front door of the research
funnel: every candidate that reaches sourcing spend passed through here first.

## Steps
1. Run the fixed checklist against the candidate: is the category big enough, is there real pain evidence (not just
   founder interest), is there scarcity or a real gap, does it fit the brand's store model.
2. Pull the category's multi-year trend line. A candidate riding a single-year spike gets flagged, not killed outright.
3. Count existing sellers or listings in the category to read competitive saturation. A crowded category needs a
   sharper angle than an open one.
4. Score every check pass, caution or reject, each with a one-line reason a person could check.
5. Combine into one verdict. A caution needs two or more supporting checks before it proceeds; a single caution alone
   does not clear the gate.

## Checks
- Every check states its reason; "just doesn't feel right" is never a valid reason.
- The trend line is real data, not a single number from memory.
- Saturation is counted, not guessed at.

## Output
{verdict, checks[{name, result, reason}], trend_read, saturation_count}

## Example
Verdict: caution. Category size: pass ($50M category, growing). Pain evidence: pass (3 review threads, 40+ mentions
of the same complaint). Scarcity: caution (2 close competitors, no clear open gap yet). Trend: 3-year CAGR 18%.
Saturation: 34 sellers on the nearest marketplace search. Verdict rests on the differentiation workflow closing the
scarcity gap before this proceeds.

# Differentiation angle

## Purpose
Every candidate and every hero product needs one owned point of difference, not a vague "better quality" claim. This
skill turns a scouted competitor gap into a concrete angle and a small set of SKU options that build on it.

## Steps
1. Read the hero product's real performance (sales, margin, reviews) and note the category's default feature set: 
   what every competitor already does.
2. Name the single thing that differs from that default. It must trace to a specific, cited gap found during
   competitor scouting, never an invented or assumed advantage.
3. Draft 2 to 3 line-extension SKU options that build on the angle rather than duplicating the hero product.
4. Tag each option's demand pattern: evergreen, trending, or seasonal: using sales history or category norms as
   evidence, not a guess.
5. Check whether a subscription model is genuinely earned: look for real repeat_rate_90d/365d data. Absent that
   evidence, tag the SKU a one-time purchase, never assume recurring revenue.

## Checks
- The angle names a specific competitor gap it closes, with a citation.
- Every line-extension option states exactly what it adds over the hero SKU.
- The subscription verdict rests on repeat-purchase data, never founder preference.

## Output
{angle, line_extension_options[{name, adds, demand_tag, evidence}], subscription_fit}

## Example
Angle: "every competitor ships a fixed-size travel kit; ours is the only one with 3 refill sizes." Options: refill
2-pack (evergreen), holiday gift box (seasonal, Q4 spike from 2 prior years' data; india: festive gift
box, Diwali spike; markets: IN), travel mini (trending, but
subscription not earned: repeat_rate_90d is 4%, below the 15% floor).

# Margin, compliance and channel gate

## Purpose
No candidate reaches sourcing or listing spend without a real, computed margin and a clean compliance read. This
gate replaces founder taste and course-learned rules of thumb with the brand's own numbers.

## Steps
1. Pull every cost input from its real source: unit cost from the quote, freight and duty from the landed cost
   model, financing cost from the payment-terms structure. Pull the brand's own stated margin floor, never an
   industry rule of thumb.
2. Compute gross margin and contribution margin in code from these inputs.
3. Run the compliance screen for the category: shelf-life, regulatory certification, labelling requirements. A
   missing certification is a fail, not a caveat.
4. If the candidate targets more than the home market, score each expansion market separately on its own cost and
   price data: never assume the home market's gate result carries over.
5. Apply the remaining go-live gates together: are the claims provable, is there a real owned difference, does the
   candidate clear the brand's own thresholds, is there enough contribution margin left for ad-cost headroom.

## Checks
- Every input has a named source; a missing input blocks the gate outright rather than defaulting to zero or an
  assumption.
- The margin floor is the brand's own, cited to the decision or record that set it.
- No arithmetic is done in prose; everything routes through the landed cost calculator.

## Output
{gate, margin{gross, contribution}, compliance_flags[], per_market[], blocking_inputs[]}

## Example
Gate: fail. Contribution margin 11%, below the brand's 18% floor. Compliance: FDA facility registration not yet filed for this
SKU category: blocking (india: FSSAI licence not yet filed; markets: IN). Recommendation: hold until packaging cost drops or price rises; do not proceed to RFQ.

# Build tech pack, BOM and packaging spec

## Purpose
Vague specs cause factory disputes and sample failures. This skill writes the exact, versioned document a factory
builds to, so any downstream dispute has a written reference to check against.

## Steps
1. Write every physical dimension with a stated tolerance band. A number with no tolerance is not a spec.
2. Build the bill of materials at the component level: each component gets its own spec line and target cost, not
   one blended unit-cost figure.
3. Price packaging as its own cost line, separate from the product's unit cost, so a packaging change never hides
   inside a "unit cost went up" surprise later.
4. Assign a version number to the whole pack and log it against the SKU record. Every future sample, RFQ and PO
   references this version number, never a verbal description.
5. Book the drop-test, tamper-evidence and transit-durability test the packaging design needs, sized to the actual
   transit mode (air, sea, last-mile courier). Track the result against a stated pass criterion.
6. If the test fails, revise the spec, bump the version number, and re-book the test. Never edit the failed version
   in place.

## Checks
- Every measurement carries a tolerance band.
- Packaging appears as its own cost line in every downstream cost model.
- A durability test is booked and resolved before the SKU proceeds to production, not after a shipment already
  failed in transit.

## Output
{tech_pack_version, dimensions[{name, value, tolerance}], bom[], packaging{spec, cost, test_result}}

## Example
Tech pack v3 (v2 failed the drop test at 90cm). Box wall thickness raised from 3mm to 4.5mm corrugate, packaging cost
line up $0.35/unit. Re-booked drop test passed at 120cm. Version 3 is the one cited in the next RFQ.

# Source a spec through supplier discovery

## Purpose
This is the parent procedure for finding a supplier. The mechanics of discovery differ sharply by region: different
platforms, different verification norms, different negotiating culture: so this skill routes to a region-specific
child rather than running one generic funnel everywhere. The brand's default sourcing region is US domestic; China
and India are the other two supported regions.

## Steps
1. Read the spec's stated region preference (or the brand's default sourcing region) and select the matching child
   skill: `prod/source/us-domestic`, `prod/source/china`, or `prod/source/india`.
2. Run that child's discovery funnel: broad platform search against the exact spec, messaging a wide shortlist on
   identical terms.
3. Verify every top responder with a live video call and a certification document check: never add a supplier to
   the verified list on written claims alone.
4. If a sourcing agent is used instead of contacting a factory directly, vet the agent to the same standard as a
   factory: verified references, a live call, checkable past shipments.
5. For an open, ongoing spec, leave it running in the background against the region's own major platforms so a
   better or new supplier surfaces without a person re-running the search by hand.

## Checks
- The region-specific child procedure was used, not a generic one.
- Every verified supplier passed a video call and a certification check.
- The background watch only produces an alert; it never contacts a supplier on its own.

## Output
{shortlist[], verified[], agent_vetting[], watch_alert}

## Example
Spec: 500ml insulated bottle, MOQ 3,000. Region: India (markets: IN). Ran `prod/source/india` against IndiaMART;
shortlist of 14, verified 3 by video call and BIS certificate check, one sourcing agent vetted against two of his
past client shipments before being trusted with outreach. For a US-domestic brand, the same spec instead runs
`prod/source/us-domestic` against ThomasNet and Maker's Row.

# Source domestically in the US

## Purpose
US-domestic sourcing runs through different directories and a different first filter than overseas sourcing:
business registration and state licensing matter immediately, and category-specific certification (UL for
electrical goods, FDA for food or cosmetics, CPSC for children's products) gates a supplier before price is
discussed. This is the brand's default sourcing region.

## Steps
1. Search ThomasNet, Maker's Row and, for finished-goods wholesale rather than manufacturing, Faire or Tundra
   against the exact spec, not a loose category term.
2. Filter on business registration, EIN and any state manufacturing or trade licence first: an unregistered
   supplier is a compliance risk before it is a quality risk.
3. Message the shortlist with identical spec text, stating unit pricing and MOQ tiers up front.
4. Verify the top responders with a live video call or a facility visit, and request the certification the
   category requires (UL for electrical/hardware, FDA for food-contact or cosmetics, CPSC for children's
   products).
5. Confirm real production capacity against the stated MOQ: ask for evidence of a comparable past order, not
   just a catalogue claim of capacity.

## Checks
- Business registration and licence status are checked before outreach proceeds.
- The certification checked matches the category's actual requirement, not a generic list.
- Capacity is confirmed with evidence, never assumed from a listing.

## Output
{shortlist[], verified[{name, business_registration, certification, capacity_confirmed}]}

## Example
Spec: FDA-regulated snack packaging. Shortlist of 7 from ThomasNet; 2 verified suppliers both hold current state
food-manufacturing licences (checked against the state registry) and FDA facility registration; one showed a
comparable 5,000-unit order as capacity evidence.

# Draft RFQ and compare quotes

## Purpose
An RFQ sent with different terms to different suppliers produces quotes that cannot be honestly compared. This
skill enforces one structured request and one apples-to-apples comparison.

## Steps
1. Translate the versioned tech pack into a structured RFQ. State tolerance bands plainly: a supplier who cannot
   hold a tolerance should say so at quote time, not after the first production run.
2. Send the identical RFQ to every supplier on the shortlist, with the same requested volume tiers and the same
   response deadline.
3. Collect quotes across every requested tier. A supplier who only quotes one tier gets asked again before being
   compared.
4. Flag any quote missing a required certification or payment term; exclude it from the comparison until the gap
   is resolved.
5. Build the landed cost per unit for every quote at every tier (working with the landed cost calculator), and
   compare both unit cost and the cash impact of committing to a larger tier. Recommend one supplier and tier with
   the numbers shown, not just a lowest-price pick.

## Checks
- Every RFQ measurement matches the tech pack's own tolerance band.
- Every supplier quoted against the same terms and deadline.
- A flagged, incomplete quote never enters the final recommendation.

## Output
{rfq_document, quotes[{supplier, tier, price, terms}], flags[], recommendation}

## Example
RFQ sent to 4 verified suppliers for tiers 3,000 / 8,000 / 15,000 units. One quote flagged for missing a required UL/FDA certificate (india: a BIS
certificate; markets: IN). Recommendation: Supplier B at the 8,000 tier: lowest landed cost per unit among complete quotes, and
the cash impact fits the brand's stated cash cover.

# Run the 3-stage sample gate

## Purpose
No creative shoot, price commitment or launch date happens before a sample from the exact factory clears this gate
against an approved reference. Working from memory or a photo instead of a physical reference produces drift no one
notices until a full production run fails.

## Steps
1. Confirm the approved reference sample is physically in-house before starting any comparison. If it only exists
   at the factory, stop and get it shipped first.
2. Run the 3-stage comparison: pre-production sample against reference, production sample against reference, and a
   pulled sample from the actual shipped batch against reference. Compare side by side on every dimension the tech
   pack specifies.
3. Score the factory's communication and reliability during the round: response time to questions, accuracy of
   what they claimed versus what arrived: separate from the physical sample's quality.
4. Record pass, hold or reject for each stage, with the exact deviation stated as a measurement (e.g., "wall
   thickness 2.1mm vs. spec 3mm ± 0.2mm"), never as an impression.

## Checks
- No stage begins without a confirmed, physical in-house reference.
- Every stage has a recorded result, none skipped.
- Every deviation is a number against the tech pack, not a subjective note.

## Output
{stage_results[{stage, result, deviation}], reliability_score, overall}

## Example
Stage 1: pass. Stage 2: hold: zipper pull 4mm shorter than spec, reference confirmed 6mm minimum. Factory
responded to the flag within 24 hours with a corrected sample. Stage 2 re-run: pass. Overall: pass, logged with the
one recorded deviation and its resolution.

# Negotiate a cost-down with real leverage

## Purpose
Asking for a discount with no leverage rarely moves price and can damage the relationship. This skill builds real
leverage first, then negotiates from it, and never asks for a cost-down that would strain the relationship for more
than it is worth.

## Steps
1. Build real leverage before asking for anything: a vetted, willing alternate factory at a comparable or better
   price; a teardown of a competitor's comparable product showing where cost could come out; the category's normal
   factory margin so an ask is grounded in what is realistic, not arbitrary.
2. Present the ask with the specific leverage named plainly: "we have a comparable quote at X" carries far more
   weight than "can you do better."
3. Confirm the final price and terms in writing before treating the negotiation as closed.
4. Book the production slot at the exact factory that passed the sample gate: never a sister factory or a
   different production line, even if it is cheaper.

## Checks
- The leverage used is real: a vetted alternate that genuinely exists, not an empty threat.
- The booked slot is confirmed at the exact factory and line that passed the sample.

## Output
{leverage[], ask, outcome{price, terms}, slot_booked}

## Example
Leverage: a verified backup factory quoted 8% lower for the same spec. Ask presented with that quote referenced.
Outcome: factory matched within 3%, citing relationship history; final terms locked at 30/70 split. Slot booked for
week 6 at the same factory that passed the sample.

# Monitor supplier performance and commodity cost

## Purpose
A supplier vetted once at onboarding can still drift. This skill runs the standing, ongoing side of the
relationship: a real scorecard on delivery and quality, and a watch on the commodity inputs that quietly move a
SKU's cost even when the supplier's own price stays flat.

## Steps
1. Score every active supplier on a fixed set of measures: on-time delivery rate, defect rate, responsiveness to
   queries, and price stability over time. Use the supplier's actual order history, never an impression from the
   last conversation.
2. Track the priced-in commodity inputs behind each SKU (cotton, resin, steel, whatever the product depends on) on
   a set monthly cadence, comparing against public commodity price indices.
3. When a cost-down looks possible, weigh it against the relationship-risk cost: a supplier pushed too hard on
   price may cut corners elsewhere or deprioritize the brand's orders during a capacity crunch.
4. Flag the result for the founder where the recommendation is "hold off" rather than "push," since that is the
   less obvious call.

## Checks
- The scorecard is built from real order data, not opinion.
- A commodity flag names the specific input and the specific price move, with its date.
- Any recommendation states which risk it is weighing against which saving.

## Output
{scorecard{on_time, defect_rate, responsiveness, price_stability}, commodity_flags[], risk_recommendation}

## Example
Scorecard: on-time 94%, defect rate 1.2%, responsiveness 18-hour average, price stable 6 months. Commodity flag:
input resin up 9% this month per index. Recommendation: hold on renegotiating this supplier's price given their
strong on-time record; absorb the resin move for one cycle and recheck next month.

# Structure payment terms and cash impact

## Purpose
The payment route and split on a sourcing deal is a real cash decision, not paperwork. This skill picks the route
that matches the actual relationship risk and hands Finance the full cash picture at every deal close, never a
verbal estimate.

## Steps
1. Choose the payment route: wire transfer, letter of credit, platform trade assurance, or escrow: based on the
   supplier relationship's real history and risk, not a fixed default used for every deal.
2. Structure the split: advance percentage, balance on shipment or delivery, and any retention held back pending
   the sample or inspection result. Confirm the MOQ this split assumes.
3. Compute, in code, the float days (time cash is committed before goods or revenue arrive), the total cash locked
   up at any point in the cycle, and any financing cost if the route involves one (LC fees, trade-assurance
   charges).
4. Package the full numbers into a packet Finance can act on immediately, without needing to ask a follow-up
   question.

## Checks
- The route chosen matches the relationship's actual risk level, stated explicitly.
- Every float, cash-locked and financing figure is computed, never estimated in prose.

## Output
{route, split{advance, balance, retention}, moq, float_days, cash_locked, financing_cost}

## Example
Route: trade assurance (2-year relationship, but first order above $6,000). Split: 30% advance / 70% on shipment.
MOQ 5,000. Float: 21 days average. Cash locked at peak: $5,750. Financing cost: $0 (no LC needed). Packet sent to
Finance same day as deal close.

# Clear a shipment for departure

## Purpose
A shipment that leaves uninspected, on the wrong freight mode, or with a 3PL picked on price alone turns into a
launch-date or cash problem weeks later. This skill runs the pre-departure checklist as one gate.

## Steps
1. Book third-party inspection before the container leaves the factory: never after it has already shipped.
2. Size the acceptable defect buffer from this specific SKU's own defect history, not an industry-standard flat
   percentage. A SKU with a clean history gets a tighter buffer; one with past issues gets a wider one and closer
   scrutiny.
3. Record a disposition decision for every defective unit the inspection finds: rework, discount-and-ship, or
   discard. No unit is left undecided.
4. Pick the freight mode: air, sea, or a hybrid split: based on the shipment's weight, the launch date it needs
   to hit, and the cash the brand has available to cover air freight's premium.
5. Select the 3PL on service history (on-time rate, damage rate) rather than the lowest quote, and check
   cross-border duty thresholds and paperwork before committing to the booking.

## Checks
- The defect buffer is sized from the SKU's own real history, not a generic figure.
- The 3PL selection cites service history, not just price.
- Cross-border thresholds are checked before the shipment is booked, not discovered at customs.

## Output
{inspection_result, disposition_log[], freight_mode, threepl, threshold_check}

## Example
Inspection found 2.1% defects (buffer was set at 3% from history): all disposed as discount-and-ship. Freight:
hybrid (60% sea to save cash, 40% air to hit the launch date). 3PL selected on a 97% on-time history despite a 4%
higher quote than the cheapest bidder. Duty threshold checked and cleared before booking.

# Audit the sourcing base and watch billing/SLA

## Purpose
Two different jobs share one owner: a one-time full audit when a brand comes on board or a client is taken over,
and a standing, ongoing watch on every bill and SLA so a quiet rate increase or missed service level is never
discovered by accident.

## Steps
1. On onboarding, audit the entire sourcing base in one pass: every active supplier, their current term, their
   current price, cross-checked against what the brand's own records say should be true.
2. At a high SKU count, move purchase orders from a weekly to a daily cadence so no reorder waits an unnecessary
   week.
3. Watch every recurring supplier, courier and 3PL bill against its contracted rate, computed in code, every
   billing cycle.
4. Flag a quiet rate increase, a duplicate charge, or a new surcharge the same cycle it appears: never let it run
   for months unnoticed.
5. Track 3PL and warehouse SLA performance daily against the written SLA: pick-and-pack speed, mis-ship rate,
   damage rate, backorder rate.

## Checks
- The onboarding audit covers every active supplier, none skipped.
- Every billing check compares against the actual contracted rate, not simply against last month's bill.
- An SLA breach is flagged the day it happens, not discovered at a monthly review.

## Output
{onboarding_audit[], po_cadence, billing_flags[], sla_log[]}

## Example
Onboarding audit of 22 suppliers found one still billing an old, since-superseded rate. Billing watch flagged a
new "fuel surcharge" line from a courier this cycle, absent from the signed contract. SLA log shows the 3PL's
mis-ship rate at 0.4%, within the written 0.5% SLA.

# Trace a defect to its batch and run CAPA

## Purpose
A defect complaint that only gets logged as "SKU X has issues" cannot be fixed at the source. This skill traces the
complaint to the exact production run, using the tech pack's own version history, and runs a real corrective-action
loop with the supplier rather than accepting a verbal promise.

## Steps
1. Trace the defect complaint back to the exact production batch or lot, using the tech pack's version history and
   any batch codes on the product or packaging.
2. Once the batch is identified, check whether other units from the same batch generated complaints, to size the
   real exposure rather than treating this as an isolated incident.
3. Run the corrective-action loop with the supplier: identify the root cause together, agree the specific fix, and
   set a verification method (a re-inspection, a sample from the next run) before closing the loop.
4. Confirm the fix is actually verified: a supplier's claim that "it's fixed" does not close a CAPA; a checked,
   verified outcome does.

## Checks
- The trace names a specific batch or lot number, never just the SKU.
- The corrective action has a documented root cause, not just a fix.
- The loop only closes once verification confirms the fix, not on the supplier's word alone.

## Output
{batch_trace, root_cause, fix, verification_result}

## Example
3 complaints traced to batch #B-0447 (tech pack v4). Root cause: a die wear issue past its replacement interval.
Fix: die replaced, replacement schedule tightened. Verification: next batch's pre-shipment inspection showed zero
recurrence on the same measurement point.

# Compute reorder point and channel replenishment

## Purpose
A reorder point sized from trailing sales alone misses peak-season demand spikes (Q4, BFCM, Prime Day) and, for a
brand that offers cash-on-delivery (india only; markets: IN), the reversal risk from RTO reversing what looked
like a sale. It also misses
that Amazon FBA has its own IPI and storage limits that can block a restock even when stock is genuinely needed.
India: the spike-risk adjustment additionally accounts for festive-season demand surges and COD-market RTO
(markets: IN, reads null for a card/BNPL-only US brand).

## Steps
1. Pull real velocity and real lead time per SKU per channel. A subscription or bundle SKU uses its committed
   cadence (what customers actually signed up for), never trailing sales, since trailing sales lag a subscription's
   real demand.
2. Compute reorder point and safety stock in code, with an explicit adjustment for peak-season spike risk: Q4
   holiday and BFCM demand surges, and the reversal risk from any carrier return-to-sender or high-return-rate
   period (India: festive-season demand surges and the reversal risk from COD RTO; markets: IN).
3. Compare current stock against the computed reorder point and flag any SKU already below it or projected to fall
   below it within the lead time window.
4. For Amazon SKUs, size the FBA replenishment shipment from a real inventory-cover target, treating a stockout as
   the failure mode to avoid above almost any other cost. Check the current IPI score and storage limits before
   finalizing the shipment size, since a low IPI score can cap how much can be sent in.

## Checks
- Velocity and lead time are real, current numbers, never a stale default.
- The spike-risk adjustment is shown explicitly, not folded silently into the number.
- An IPI or storage-limit flag is raised before it blocks a planned restock, not after.

## Output
{sku, reorder_point, safety_stock, current_stock, status, fba_cover, ipi_flag}

## Example
SKU-1042: velocity 40/day, lead time 18 days, BFCM-adjusted safety stock +35%. Reorder point 1,080 units;
current stock 950: status: reorder now. FBA cover target 45 days; IPI score 420 (above the 400 threshold): no
restock block. India: the same SKU's festive-adjusted safety stock uses the same +35% logic against COD RTO risk
(markets: IN).

# Flag concentration risk and dead stock, refresh landed cost

## Purpose
Two structural risks share one owner because both are about catching a slow-moving problem before it becomes an
expensive one: too much dependence on one supplier or country, and stock quietly ageing past the point it can be
sold at full price.

## Steps
1. Compute the share of spend or volume concentrated in any single supplier or country.
2. For any concentration above the brand's own threshold, confirm a real, vetted backup supplier exists in a
   second country: not just a name on a list, but a verified alternate from the sourcing skill.
3. Recompute landed cost the moment price, freight, FX or duty actually changes, rather than waiting for a fixed
   monthly calendar date, since a duty change can move margin materially overnight.
4. Watch stock age against velocity across every channel the SKU sells on, and flag a SKU against the long-term
   storage or dead-stock threshold before it becomes dead weight, not after.
5. Draft markdown, bundle, or discontinue options for a flagged SKU, each with its cash impact computed, so the
   founder is deciding between real numbers, not vague options.

## Checks
- Every backup supplier named is real and vetted, never an assumption.
- Landed cost is recomputed on an actual triggering event, not just a fixed calendar.
- Every clearance option's cash impact is computed, not estimated.

## Output
{concentration{}, backup_confirmed, refreshed_landed_cost, dead_stock_alerts[], clearance_options[]}

## Example
Concentration: 68% of SKU-1042's spend is with one supplier in one country: above the 50% threshold; a verified
backup in a second country exists. Landed cost refreshed after a 4% duty change, margin down 1.1pt. Dead-stock
alert: SKU-0810 at 210 days of stock against a 90-day threshold; clearance options drafted at 3 markdown depths
with cash impact for each.

# Sync multi-channel stock and plan peak-season capacity

## Purpose
A stock pool split across channels without buffers oversells the moment two channels sell the last unit at once.
And a peak season fails in whichever of stock, staffing or system capacity was not planned for, not necessarily
the one that got the most attention. This skill keeps the pool synced day to day and plans for the season as one
combined picture. India: the same plan is built around the festive calendar (Diwali, wedding season) instead of
BFCM/Q4 (markets: IN).

## Steps
1. Keep one stock pool synced across every channel: site, marketplaces, rapid-delivery platforms, physical stores:
with a stated buffer per channel that prevents any one channel from overselling against real available stock.
2. Set order-routing and split-shipment rules by channel and warehouse, so an order is fulfilled from the right
location without a person deciding case by case.
3. Ahead of Q4/BFCM, project the safety stock the season will need using at least one prior peak cycle's data
where it exists, not a flat percentage bump (India: ahead of the festive season; markets: IN).
4. Check warehouse staffing and WMS/OMS system load against that projected peak volume, expressed as a percentage
of capacity used, not a yes/no guess.
5. Combine stock, staffing and system-load readiness into one plan, since a plan that only covers stock misses the
two failure modes that actually cause a bad peak season.

## Checks
- No channel is allowed to oversell against its stated buffer.
- The readiness plan explicitly covers stock, staffing and system load together, not stock alone.

## Output
{sync_status, routing_rules[], peak_projection, capacity_check, readiness_plan}

## Example
Buffers set: site 5%, marketplaces 8% (slower stock sync), rapid-delivery platforms 15% (fastest depletion risk).
Peak projection: BFCM week needs 2.4x baseline safety stock based on last year's data. Staffing check: current
warehouse shift covers 78% of projected peak pick volume: flagged for an extra shift. India: the same brand's
Diwali-week projection runs on the festive calendar instead (markets: IN).

# Select 3PL/WMS and build warehouse and returns operations

## Purpose
Three related decisions belong to one fulfilment manager: which 3PL and WMS to run on, how the warehouse actually
operates day to day, and what happens to every unit that comes back. Keeping them together avoids a WMS chosen
without the warehouse rules it needs to support, or a returns rule invented case by case after go-live.

## Steps
1. Run the RFP and SLA negotiation for a domestic fulfilment 3PL (ShipStation/EasyPost-connected, or a 3PL such as
ShipBob or ShipMonk): separate from any import-side freight or factory 3PL, since the requirements differ
(last-mile speed and accuracy versus long-haul cost).
2. Test the 3PL's WMS integration before go-live: order sync, stock sync, and returns feed, all tested end to end.
3. Set slotting rules by SKU velocity (fast movers closest to pack stations) and the pick-pack-QC method and
staffing level against real, not projected, order volume.
4. Design a fixed rule for what happens to every returned unit: a carrier return-to-sender or a customer return
(India: RTO or customer return; markets: IN): restock, refurbish, or write off, decided in advance rather than
case by case, and apply it on a set schedule.
5. Review staffing levels and grading outcomes weekly against the plan.

## Checks
- The 3PL is chosen on SLA terms and service history, not the lowest quote alone.
- Go-live never happens before the WMS integration test passes.
- The grading rule is fixed and decided in advance, never improvised per return.

## Output
{sla, integration_test_result, slotting_rules, staffing_plan, grading_ruleset}

## Example
3PL selected on a 96% on-time SLA history despite a 5% higher quote. Integration test passed on stock sync;
returns feed needed a fix before go-live. Grading rule: return-to-sender with unopened seal restocks
automatically; opened seal goes to refurbish queue; anything past 60 days is written off. India: the equivalent
rule applies to RTO instead (markets: IN).

# Run daily carrier rate-shop and failed-delivery resolution

## Purpose
A fixed default carrier for every shipment ignores real, live differences in rate, serviceability and reliability by zone. And a carrier exception (address issue, failed attempt) left unworked past the delivery window becomes a return-to-sender that did not need to happen. This skill runs both the routing decision and the same-day exception response as one daily operating rhythm. India: the same daily rhythm runs as NDR (non-delivery report) resolution on cash-on-delivery orders (markets: IN, reads null for US brands).

## Steps
1. Pick the carrier for each shipment in code, from live rate, ZIP code serviceability, and the carrier's own SLA history in that specific zone (UPS, USPS, FedEx, or a connected 3PL such as ShipBob or ShipMonk): never a single fixed default carrier used everywhere.
2. Fail over automatically to a backup carrier the moment the primary fails serviceability or its SLA for that shipment, without waiting for a manual check.
3. Pull every carrier exception raised today, run USPS/carrier address validation, and confirm the address or reschedule delivery with the customer by SMS (TCPA consent, quiet hours) or email before the carrier's own attempt window closes (India: pull the aggregator's NDR queue and confirm by SMS or WhatsApp; markets: IN).
4. Log the outcome of every routing decision and every exception resolution, and flag any zone showing a rising return-to-sender trend for the monthly carrier scorecard (India: a rising NDR or RTO trend; markets: IN).

## Checks
- Every carrier choice is computed from live data, never defaulted to one fixed carrier.
- Every exception raised today is worked the same day, before its attempt window closes.

## Output
{carrier_choice, failover_event, exception_outcomes[]}

## Example
Order routed to UPS on best rate/SLA for ZIP 10001; UPS's API reported non-serviceable mid-day, failed over automatically to USPS. Same-day exception queue: 14 items, 11 resolved by address confirmation, 2 rescheduled, 1 marked return-to-sender after 2 failed contact attempts. India: same day's NDR queue for pincode 400001 worked the same way, 1 marked RTO (markets: IN).

# Score couriers and draft a renegotiation

## Purpose
Carrier volume should shift to whoever is actually performing better, on real and sustained evidence, not on one
bad week. And a renegotiation ask lands better with a real, cited benchmark behind it than with a bare complaint
about cost.

## Steps
1. Update the running scorecard per carrier per zone: failed-delivery/return-to-sender rate, first-attempt
delivery rate, transit time, using the same measurement window for every carrier being compared (India: RTO rate
per courier per pincode zone; markets: IN).
2. Compare zone performance across carriers and shift volume to the better performer only where the gap is real
and sustained across more than one measurement period, not a single good or bad week.
3. Watch the brand's own shipping cost per order against public rate benchmarks for comparable carriers (UPS,
USPS, FedEx, regional 3PLs; India: comparable India couriers; markets: IN), on a set cadence.
4. When cost drifts meaningfully above benchmark, or a contract renewal is approaching, draft a renegotiation ask
with the specific, dated benchmark evidence attached.

## Checks
- A volume shift is only recommended on a sustained gap across more than one period.
- Every renegotiation ask cites a real, dated public rate card, not a vague sense that cost feels high.

## Output
{scorecard{}, volume_shift, benchmark_read, renegotiation_draft}

## Example
Carrier A: 96% first-attempt in Zone North, sustained 3 months. Carrier B: 89%, also sustained. Recommendation:
shift 15% of Zone North volume from B to A. Cost-per-order benchmark: brand paying 8% above the current published
average for comparable weight/zone carriers: renegotiation draft cites the specific rate card and date.

# File courier and marketplace claims

## Purpose
Money owed for a lost, damaged, or wrongly billed unit is only recovered if someone files the claim with proof and
tracks it to payout. This skill covers both carrier-side claims (lost/damaged shipments) and marketplace-side
claims (FBA reimbursements, Walmart/eBay/TikTok Shop claim programs; india: Flipkart SPF, Myntra claims) with the
same discipline: proof first, then file, then track.

## Steps
1. Identify every shipment marked lost, damaged, or wrongly marked return-to-sender in the review period (india:
wrongly marked RTO; markets: IN).
2. Assemble proof for each: photos of the package or product condition, any weight discrepancy against the
   shipping manifest, seal condition on return.
3. File the courier claim with the carrier or aggregator, proof attached, within their stated filing window.
4. Separately, find lost or damaged marketplace inventory and any wrongly charged fee inside each seller console,
   and file the matching reimbursement claim type for that platform (FBA reimbursement, Walmart Seller Center
   claim, eBay/TikTok Shop claim; india: Flipkart SPF, Myntra claim).
5. Track payout against every open claim: a claim is only marked paid once the payout is actually confirmed, not
   simply once it is filed.
6. Escalate any claim that has passed its normal resolution window.

## Checks
- No claim is filed without an attached proof packet.
- Payout status reflects confirmed payment, never an assumption.

## Output
{incident_list[], filed_claims[], payout_tracker[], escalations[]}

## Example
3 shipments this week marked damaged; proof (photos, weight mismatch) assembled and filed with the carrier.
Separately, an FBA reimbursement claim filed for 2 units lost in an Amazon warehouse, confirmed paid within 12
days. One carrier claim escalated after exceeding its 15-day resolution window.

# Handle a non-standard operations request

## Purpose
Four event types: a first export order, a pop-up or stockist deal, a safety recall, and a made-to-order sale: 
are each rare enough that no single standard workflow covers them, but common enough across a brand's life that
each deserves its own real procedure rather than being improvised from scratch every time. This parent skill
classifies the request and routes to the matching child.

## Steps
1. Read the triggering event and classify it as exactly one type: export, offline retail, recall, or
   made-to-order. A request that seems to match two types is split into two separate runs.
2. Route to the matching child skill (`prod/non-standard-ops/export`, `/offline-retail`, `/recall`, or
   `/made-to-order`) and run its specific procedure.
3. Run the compliance check appropriate to that type (export duty rules, retail licensing, regulator notification,
   or custom-order terms).
4. Document the full handling, including any customer communication, and log the outcome to the registry.

## Checks
- Exactly one type is classified per request.
- A recall never proceeds past classification without reaching the founder gate first.

## Output
{type, packet, compliance_result, documentation}

## Example
Event: a customer signs up for a pop-up in a new city. Classified: offline_retail. Routed to the offline-retail
child, which set up POS, consignment terms and a daily reconciliation schedule for the event's duration.

# Cross-border compliance: US customs, tariffs and international shipping

## Purpose
A first international sourcing shipment or a first outbound international order each has its own paperwork and
duty-exposure decisions that a domestic shipment never touches. Getting the incoterm wrong surprises the buyer
with an unexpected duty bill and damages the relationship on the very first order; getting an HTS classification
wrong on an inbound shipment causes a customs hold or a duty overpayment. India: the equivalent event is an export
from India, which instead needs IEC and LUT registration for zero-rated GST (markets: IN, reads null for US
brands).

## Steps
1. For an inbound sourcing shipment, secure a customs bond (continuous or single-entry) and classify each product
by its correct HTS code against the current US tariff schedule.
2. Check tariff exposure for that HTS code and country of origin, and whether the shipment qualifies for Section
321 de minimis entry (currently for shipments under $800 per person per day) to avoid duty and formal entry where
eligible.
3. For an outbound international order, prepare the commercial invoice and the carrier's export paperwork,
matching HTS/HS codes and shipment value exactly, and choose DDP (duty paid by the seller) or DDU (duty paid by
the buyer) so the buyer's total cost is clear before they order, not discovered at their own customs.
4. India (markets: IN): set up IEC (Import Export Code) and LUT (Letter of Undertaking) so exports can be
zero-rated for GST, and determine HS codes against the destination country's tariff schedule instead of the US's.

## Checks
- HTS/HS codes are checked against the actual current schedule, not assumed from a prior shipment's code.
- The incoterm choice is communicated to the buyer before the order ships, not after.

## Output
{customs_bond_status, hts_codes[], tariff_exposure, section_321_eligible, commercial_invoice, incoterm, export_paperwork}

## Example
Inbound shipment from a China supplier, value $18,000: continuous customs bond confirmed active, HTS code checked
against the current schedule, tariff exposure computed, does not qualify for Section 321 given per-shipment value.
Outbound order to Canada: incoterm DDP chosen so the buyer sees one all-in price with no duty surprise on
delivery. India: first order to UAE instead runs on IEC/LUT (markets: IN), HS code checked against UAE's tariff
schedule, incoterm DDP chosen the same way.

# Offline retail, stockist and pop-up operations

## Purpose
A pop-up, exhibition or stockist arrangement moves real physical stock outside the normal warehouse-to-courier
flow, and needs its own POS, its own stock accounting, and its own daily discipline so nothing is lost between
what left the warehouse and what actually sold or came back.

## Steps
1. Set up point-of-sale for the event or the stockist location.
2. Run the stock transfer to the location, and track any returns or unsold stock coming back.
3. Reconcile consignment settlement (what the stockist owes for what actually sold) and daily sales for the
   duration of the event.
4. Run the staff roster for the event, matched to expected footfall.

## Checks
- Daily reconciliation happens every single day of the event, not only at the end.
- Every unit transferred out is matched against a unit sold or a unit returned; nothing is unaccounted for.

## Output
{pos_setup, stock_transfer_log, daily_reconciliation[], settlement}

## Example
3-day pop-up: 400 units transferred. Daily reconciliation each day matched sales against POS records. Final
settlement: 340 sold, 55 returned unsold, 5 flagged as a discrepancy for follow-up with the venue.

# Product recall and safety incident procedure

## Purpose
A safety-related defect is the single highest-stakes event this agent can face. This procedure exists to make sure
speed and completeness happen together: sale stops everywhere immediately, every affected buyer is found and
contacted, and every regulator notice is logged, with the founder in the loop from the first step.

## Steps
1. Find every affected batch using the tech pack's own versioning and any production batch codes.
2. Stop sale on every channel: site, every marketplace, quick commerce: immediately, before any other step in
   this procedure proceeds.
3. Contact every buyer who purchased an affected batch, using purchase records, and arrange a return or
   replacement.
4. Log every regulator notice received or filed in connection with the incident.

## Checks
- Sale is stopped on every channel before any other action, with no exception.

  agent judgment alone.

contacted with replacement offers. One regulator notice logged and filed as required.

# Screen an Amazon opportunity and mine reviews/keywords

## Purpose
A candidate that cleared the general product screen (PROD-C01-C05) still needs Amazon-specific diligence: Amazon's
own price dynamics, keyword search behaviour, and review patterns work differently from the open web or DTC.

## Steps
1. Apply Amazon-specific elimination screens: a price floor below which margin cannot work after fees, the price
   spread across page-1 listings (a huge spread signals a confusing or commoditized category), keyword search
   variability, and how dominant one or two brands already are in the category.
2. Run a real fad filter against the candidate's Amazon search trend data: a single-month spike is not the same
   as sustained demand.
3. Read 1 to 3 star reviews on the closest competing listings for complaints this candidate's design could fix. Use
   the complaint as a design input, never copy the review's wording into any copy.
4. Confirm mid-rated, high-volume sellers exist in the category as a demand-and-gap signal: real search volume
   with real dissatisfaction is the strongest opportunity signal available.
5. Mine keywords from reverse-ASIN tools for the category, ranked by search volume where the tool provides it.

## Checks
- Every elimination screen states its specific reason.
- The fad filter is based on more than one data point over time.
- No review text is copied verbatim; only the underlying gap it points to is used.

## Output
{screen_result, fad_verdict, complaint_list[], keyword_list[]}

## Example
Screen: pass (price floor clears with FBA fees included, page-1 spread moderate). Fad filter: pass, 3-year steady
growth not a single spike. Complaints mined: "lid doesn't seal after 2 months" appears in 40+ reviews across 3
competitors: a fixable design input. Keywords ranked by volume for the listing build.

# Model Amazon channel economics

## Purpose
Amazon's referral fee, FBA fee and storage cost stack up in ways that are easy to underestimate from memory. This
skill models the full stack in code against a SKU's real landed cost, so a launch or continuation decision is made
on a real net margin, not a gross-margin illusion.

## Steps
1. Pull the current, dated Amazon fee stack for the category: referral fee percentage, FBA pick-pack-ship fee by
   size tier, and storage cost by month.
2. Model the full fee stack against the SKU's landed cost, computed in code, never estimated.
3. Add a stated PPC budget assumption (clearly labeled as an assumption) and the storage cost for the SKU's actual
   size tier.
4. Check the resulting Amazon price against the brand's DTC price-parity rule, using the current live DTC price,
   not a stale one.
5. Compute net margin after every fee line, in code, and flag any SKU whose net margin falls below the brand's own
   stated floor.

## Checks
- Every fee line is sourced from Amazon's currently published rate card, dated.
- Net margin is computed in code, never estimated in prose.
- Price parity is checked against the live DTC price at the time of the check.

## Output
{fee_stack, net_margin_per_sku[], parity_check, margin_floor_flags[]}

## Example
SKU-1042: referral fee 15%, FBA fee $3.50 (size tier standard), storage $0.15/unit/month. Landed cost $8.50, Amazon
price $24.99. Net margin after all fees and a $1.50 PPC assumption: 19%, above the brand's 15% floor. Parity check:
Amazon price matches DTC within the allowed band.

# Build a marketplace listing

## Purpose
Every marketplace enforces its own title length, bullet rules, image slots and attribute set, and none of them are
the same. This is the parent procedure: it never posts a listing itself, only drafts one, and it always routes to
the platform-specific child before writing a single field. Amazon, Walmart, Target Plus, eBay and TikTok Shop are
the default US-first children; Flipkart/Myntra/Nykaa and Blinkit/Zepto are grouped India-market options (markets:
IN), not selected for a US-only brand.

## Steps
1. Confirm the target marketplace and select the matching child skill
   (`prod/list-on-marketplace/amazon`, `/walmart`, `/target-plus`, `/ebay`, `/tiktok-shop`, or, for an India brand,
   `/flipkart-myntra-nykaa` or `/blinkit-zepto`).
2. Run the child's specific field rules to place the top keyword and write benefit-led, claim-checked copy in the
   platform's own format.
3. Brief every image slot to that platform's own size, crop and content rule: an Amazon main image and a
   TikTok Shop video cover are not interchangeable.
4. Fill every attribute field the platform requires and confirm the correct category node in that platform's own
   taxonomy.
5. Package the finished draft for a named human to paste into the seller console. This skill never posts directly
   to a live listing on any platform.

## Checks
- The marketplace named is one of the seven supported children, matched to its own child procedure.
- No required field is left blank.
- Nothing produced by this skill is ever posted directly; it is always handed to a human.

## Output
{marketplace, listing_draft, image_briefs[], attributes{}, category_node}

## Example
Marketplace: target-plus. Routed to `prod/list-on-marketplace/target-plus`. Title and key callouts placed per
Target's own style guide; 5 image slots briefed to Target's spec; attributes filled; draft handed to the
marketplace manager to paste into Target Plus's Partners Online portal. India: the equivalent nykaa listing routes
to `prod/list-on-marketplace/flipkart-myntra-nykaa` instead (markets: IN).

# Check US labelling and quality-marking compliance (FTC, Care Labeling, Prop 65)

## Purpose
A marketplace can pull a listing, or worse, penalize the account, for a missing FTC precious-metal quality mark, a missing textile Care Labeling Rule disclosure, or a missing Prop 65 warning. This check runs before a listing is built, not after a takedown notice. India: the same job checks BIS hallmarking and Legal Metrology labelling instead (markets: IN, reads null for US brands).

## Steps
1. Identify which compliance requirement applies to this specific category: the FTC Jewelry Guides quality mark (precious-metal jewellery), the Care Labeling Rule (fibre content, origin, care for textiles), a Prop 65 warning, or a CPSC rule (India: BIS certification for hardware/electronics/toys, hallmarking for jewellery, or Legal Metrology labelling; markets: IN).

A real-time India BIS/hallmarking registry API was not found in the wave-2 research pass (markets: IN); that variant of this check reads a human-recorded status (BIS Care app or equivalent, checked by a person) rather than verifying a hallmark itself.

# Prepare an FBA inbound shipment

## Purpose
FBA's dimension and weight limits change, and an outdated cached limit produces a rejected or delayed shipment.
Keeping the full paper trail matters because it is the only evidence available if inventory goes missing in
Amazon's own warehouse.

## Steps
1. Measure the actual case dimensions and check them against FBA's currently published hard limits, pulled fresh
   rather than from a cached figure from a past shipment.
2. Reuse a saved shipment template whenever this SKU and case size match a shipment already sent successfully,
   to avoid re-deriving the plan from scratch each time.
3. Build the shipment plan: box count, weight per box (checked under the carrier's per-box limit), and carrier
   choice.
4. Generate and check carton labels against FBA's current label specification before printing.
5. Keep the full paper trail: bill of lading, carrier receipt, carton count: so a later lost-inventory claim has
   the evidence it needs.
6. Confirm the shipment against Amazon's inbound dashboard once it is marked received, and flag any discrepancy
   between what was sent and what was received.

## Checks
- The dimension limits used are the currently published ones, not a cached figure.
- The paper trail is complete before the shipment physically leaves.

## Output
{dimension_check, shipment_plan, carton_labels, paper_trail, receipt_confirmation}

## Example
Case dimensions checked against FBA's current oversize threshold: under by 2cm. Template reused from the last
shipment of the same SKU. 40 cartons, weight checked under the carrier's 25kg/box limit. Paper trail filed; receipt
confirmed 6 days later with a 2-unit discrepancy flagged for a claim.

# Sequence an Amazon account, Brand Registry and launch

## Purpose
Account setup, trademark filing, Brand Registry enrolment and launch-week execution have a strict order: doing
them out of order (enrolling Brand Registry before the trademark is filed, for instance) causes rejections and
weeks of delay. This skill enforces the correct sequence.

## Steps
1. Get the Amazon seller account, business entity, payout details and identity verification right the first time
: a rejected or later-flagged account costs far more time than a careful first submission.
2. Sequence trademark filing before listing creation; Brand Registry cannot be enrolled without a filed trademark,
   so this step must complete first.
3. Once the trademark is filed and the listing (built via PROD-W22) is live, enrol Brand Registry.
4. Turn on the Storefront and Subscribe & Save benefits Brand Registry unlocks, confirming both are actually live,
   not just eligible.
5. Concentrate real demand into the first launch weeks by aligning stock arrival and PPC campaign start to the same
   date, and build a pre-launch audience where the platform's rules allow it.
6. Protect a novel product against copycats from day one: watermark product images, and file for design protection
   where the product is genuinely novel.

## Checks
- No step in the sequence is attempted before its prerequisite is confirmed complete.
- Stock and PPC go live on the same date, never staggered by more than a day.

## Output
{account_status, trademark_status, brand_registry_status, launch_plan, protection_checklist}

## Example
Account verified on first submission (2 weeks). Trademark filed before listing creation. Listing built and live.
Brand Registry enrolled once both prerequisites confirmed. Launch week: stock arrived and PPC campaign started the
same day; a pre-launch waitlist built the prior 2 weeks.

# Monitor marketplace health: reviews, account health, Buy Box

## Purpose
A policy notice ignored for a week can become a suspension; an unauthorized reseller undercutting on price can
erode a brand's own margin and trust. This skill runs the standing weekly health check that keeps both from
becoming a surprise.

## Steps
1. Request product reviews only through the platform's own permitted request mechanism: never an incentivised or
   off-platform review ask, which risks policy action against the account.
2. Contest any feedback that is misplaced (attached to the wrong product) or violates the platform's own feedback
   policy, through the platform's formal dispute process.
3. Check the Account Health dashboard every single week without exception, so a new policy notice is caught the
   week it appears, not discovered a month later as a suspension.
4. Check who holds the Buy Box across every marketplace listing, and check unauthorised reseller pricing against
   the brand's own MAP (minimum advertised price) policy.
5. Flag any MAP or price-integrity problem to the founder for a decision, rather than changing the brand's own
   price unilaterally in response.

## Checks
- Every review request uses a platform-permitted method.
- No price is changed by this agent in response to a MAP issue; it is always flagged to the founder.

## Output
{review_requests[], account_health_status, buy_box_report, map_violation_flags[]}

## Example
Account Health: clear, no new notices this week. Buy Box: held on 8 of 9 active listings; the 9th lost to an
unauthorized reseller pricing 12% below the brand's MAP: flagged for the founder rather than matching the price.

# Diagnose Amazon performance and plan growth

## Purpose
A sales drop on Amazon has at least two very different causes: fewer people seeing the listing, or fewer people
buying once they see it: and confusing the two leads to the wrong fix. This skill forces that split before any
other conclusion, and keeps growth responses inside Amazon's own compliant tools.

## Steps
1. Split any sales change into a traffic component and a conversion component, using Business Reports data, before
   drawing any conclusion about the product.
2. Check attribution (is the traffic even coming from where it looks like) and seasonality (is this the normal
   pattern for this time of year) before calling a product a failure based on a raw sales number.
3. Respond only with Amazon's own compliant promotion tools: Lightning Deals, Coupons, Amazon-native ad formats: 
   never an outside workaround that risks a policy violation.
4. Decide whether to add a second SKU based on the diagnosis, not on a hunch, and test smaller situational growth
   levers (FBM to FBA conversion, Small and Light enrolment, a design-vendor bake-off, Amazon Live) each with a
   defined read set before the test starts.
5. Write the one-page memo behind any decision to add or expand the Amazon channel.

## Checks
- The traffic/conversion split happens before any conclusion about the product itself.
- Every growth-lever test has its read defined before the test starts, never decided after seeing results.

## Output
{diagnosis{traffic_change, conversion_change}, promotion_response, growth_tests[], channel_memo}

## Example
Sales down 22% week over week. Diagnosis: traffic down 3% (normal seasonality), conversion down 19%: points to a
listing or price issue, not a demand problem. Response: a compliant Coupon test with a defined 2-week read, not an
off-platform discount code.

# Build, validate and audit the catalogue feed

## Purpose
Media buyer and Organic both depend on one clean feed to plug into shopping ads and marketplace channels, and a
broken image or a duplicate SKU discovered by a channel's own rejection wastes a cycle that a standing audit would
have caught first.

## Steps
1. Keep one clean master product feed: titles, images, prices, availability, and GTIN, with no duplicate SKU and
   no missing GTIN.
2. Validate the feed against each destination channel's own current schema before handing it off: a schema that
   worked last month may have changed.
3. Hand the validated feed to Media buyer and Organic, and confirm it loaded without error on their side.
4. Run a standing audit across every channel's live listings for broken images, missing attributes, and duplicate
   SKUs that may have crept in independently of the feed.
5. Check for the brand's own price mismatch between its site and each marketplace, flagging any gap rather than
   silently reconciling it.
6. Check every new product image and video against each channel's own size, crop and content rule before it is
   pushed, since an Instacart thumbnail and an Amazon main image have entirely different requirements (india: a Blinkit
   thumbnail; markets: IN).

## Checks
- The feed has zero duplicate SKUs and zero missing GTINs before handoff.
- A price mismatch is always flagged, never quietly auto-corrected.
- Image and video specs are checked before push, not discovered via a channel's rejection.

## Output
{master_feed, validation_report, quality_audit_report, price_mismatch_report, asset_spec_flags[]}

## Example
Feed validated clean against Amazon's, Walmart's and Instacart's current schemas. Weekly audit found 3 SKUs with a
broken image link on one marketplace and a $2 price mismatch between site and Walmart: both flagged, neither
auto-corrected. India: the same audit flags a ₹20 price mismatch between site and Flipkart instead (markets: IN).

# Onboard a brand on rapid-delivery and quick-commerce platforms

## Purpose
Rapid-delivery/quick-commerce onboarding requires a specific document set and each platform runs its own review
process and its own unit-economics validation window (commonly around 90 days) before the brand is judged to be
worth investing in further. Missing a required document is the most common cause of onboarding delay. India: the
same job onboards to Blinkit, Zepto or Instamart with GST and FSSAI documents instead (markets: IN).

## Steps
1. Assemble the business licence, resale certificate, UPC/GS1 barcode and packaging documents the platform's own
onboarding checklist requires, confirming every item is present before submission (India: GST registration, FSSAI
licence, PAN, bank and GS1 barcode documents instead; markets: IN).
2. Submit through the platform's own onboarding channel (Instacart Retailer/CPG portal, DoorDash Marketplace,
Gopuff vendor channel; india: Blinkit Seller App, Zepto category-manager channel, Instamart seller portal), never
a workaround or a third-party shortcut.
3. Track the document review status and respond to any query the platform raises within its stated window.
4. Prepare the initial catalogue listing using the matching platform listing skill.
5. Confirm the platform's own unit-economics validation window and what it requires the brand to demonstrate
during it.
6. Get the brand live and confirm the first order flows correctly end to end before calling onboarding complete.

## Checks
- Every document the platform's checklist requires is present before submission.
- The validation window and its specific requirement are both logged, not assumed.

## Output
{document_packet, review_status, initial_listing, validation_window, go_live_confirmation}

## Example
Documents assembled: business licence, resale certificate, UPC registration, packaging compliance declaration.
Submitted through Instacart's Retailer portal. First order confirmed to flow correctly on day 12 of a stated
90-day validation window. India: the same brand's Blinkit onboarding instead used GST, FSSAI licence and GS1
barcode documents (markets: IN).

# Manage rapid-delivery ad credits and dark-store fill rate

## Purpose
Rapid-delivery/quick-commerce platforms typically report ROAS on list/MRP price, which overstates real return by
30 to 50 percent; judging ad spend on that number leads to bad decisions. And a dark-store stockout triggers an
algorithmic ranking penalty that takes real time to recover from, so it needs daily, not weekly, attention.

## Steps
1. Spend each platform's ad tools deliberately rather than leaving credits unused, and pull back spend for a SKU
once its organic search ranking improves and stops needing paid support.
2. Recompute ROAS from actual transaction value, never the platform's own list/MRP-based default, before judging
whether spend is working.
3. Negotiate peak promotional windows (BFCM, Prime Day, Q4 holidays; India: the festive calendar; markets: IN)
ahead of the calendar date, since terms secured early are typically better than what is available once the rush
begins.
4. Watch stock levels across the dark-store network daily, the way a merchandiser walks the shelf, and flag a
stockout before it triggers the platform's own algorithmic ranking penalty, which is slow to recover from once
triggered.

## Checks
- Every ROAS figure used for a decision is recomputed from transaction value, never quoted from the platform's
  list/MRP-based dashboard number.
- A fill-rate flag is raised before the ranking-penalty window closes, not after the penalty has already applied.

## Output
{ad_spend_plan, roas_recomputed, promo_terms, dark_store_report, stockout_flags[]}

## Example
Platform-reported ROAS: 4.2x (list-price-based). Recomputed from transaction value: 2.9x: spend plan adjusted down
for the weakest SKU. Dark-store report: 2 of 40 stores below reorder threshold, flagged same day, ahead of the
platform's ranking-penalty window.

# Track FDA, net-quantity, state licence and EPR compliance

## Purpose
FDA facility registration, Fair Packaging and Labeling Act net-quantity declarations, state licensing (cosmetics,
food, supplements) and state EPR packaging filing are each recurring, concrete obligations that a brand either
tracks deliberately or handles ad hoc under deadline pressure. This skill keeps one register instead of several
scattered across people's memory. India: the same register tracks Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities)
registration, an FSSAI licence and India's EPR plastic-packaging rules instead (markets: IN, reads null for US
brands).

## Steps
1. Keep one register listing which SKUs require FDA facility registration or a state cosmetics/food/supplement
licence, based on their actual category (India: Legal Metrology state registration or an FSSAI licence; markets:
IN).
2. Track each licence's current validity window, so an expiry is known well ahead of the date, not discovered
after it lapses.
3. Flag the relabelling a SKU needs on any formula, claim or price change: net quantity, ingredients and any
Prop 65 warning (India: on any MRP or GST change, keeping the original MRP visible as the rule requires; markets:
IN).
4. Register the brand's packaging under the relevant state's EPR rules (Oregon, California, Colorado, Maine;
India: under India's EPR rules; markets: IN), and track the annual filing deadline and recycling-target
obligation.
5. Flag when a shortfall against the recycling target means the brand needs to buy EPR credits, stating the
shortfall amount specifically.

## Checks
- Every licence's validity window reflects a checked, current status, never an assumption that it is still valid.
- A relabelling flag fires on every formula/claim/price change, not only when a licence comes up for renewal.

## Output
{licence_register[], relabelling_flags[], epr_status, epr_shortfall_flag}

## Example
Licence register: 14 of 18 SKUs require a state cosmetics licence or FDA registration, all current. One state
licence expiring in 45 days, flagged to the founder. A recent formula change on 3 SKUs triggered a relabelling
flag. Oregon EPR filing on track; no shortfall this cycle. India: the same brand's Legal Metrology/FSSAI register
and EPR filing run the equivalent check (markets: IN).

# Platform, app and automation governance

## Purpose
Keep the store's app stack lean, its small operational rules automated without custom code, and its platform surface current, all under one governance discipline.

## Steps
1. Vet any candidate app against ratings and a real before/after speed test, never install on trust alone.
2. Consolidate apps doing the same job, and search for residual theme code after every uninstall.
3. List recurring manual if-this-then-that actions a store manager does by hand.
4. Wire each into the platform's native automation layer (Shopify Flow or equivalent), never a custom-coded rule for pure logic.
5. Test each rule against a real historical order before turning it on live, and log every action it fires.
6. Read each platform release (Shopify Editions, WooCommerce/WordPress core, app deprecations, API sunsets) on its own schedule.
7. Match new native features against the paid app list to flag a possible retirement, and write a short adopt-or-ignore memo.
8. For a brand with a mobile app, QA the store listing, screenshots, deep links and push opt-in before each release.

## Checks
- Every automation rule tested against a real order before going live, with its actions logged.
- No API key or credential appears anywhere outside the platform's own secure settings.

## Output
An app audit report, working automation rules with an audit log, a short per-release memo, and (when relevant) an app release QA report.

"Automation rule: auto-tag orders over $150 with a prior chargeback or return-to-sender history as 'high-risk-review'. Tested against 20 historical orders, correctly flagged 3 known cases, enabled live."

# Build a custom integration or webhook

## Purpose
Connect the store to an ERP, warehouse system, loyalty ledger, marketplace feed or courier safely, with retries and alerting instead of a silent, brittle one-way sync.

## Steps
1. Map every field that must sync both ways (inventory, order status, tracking number, loyalty points) before writing any code.
2. Build the custom app or Shopify Flow automation and register the needed webhooks.
3. Store API keys and tokens only in the platform's secure app settings or the environment secret store, never in theme code or a public repo.
4. Add retry-with-backoff on failed webhook deliveries, with a dead-letter log for ones that never succeed.
5. Alert a human the moment a sync gap is detected (order count mismatch, stale inventory timestamp).
6. Document the data contract so a future developer does not reverse-engineer it.
7. Test against a sandbox or staging account of the external system before pointing at production.

## Checks
- No credential appears outside the platform's secure settings.
- A deliberately failed test webhook triggers the retry logic and, if it keeps failing, a human alert.

## Output
A working integration or Flow, a retry log, a written data contract, and a sync-health alert rule.

"Inventory sync to the 3PL's WMS: field-mapped SKU, quantity, location. Retry with exponential backoff up to 5 attempts, dead-letter log after that, Slack alert to ops on any dead-letter entry."

# Automated regression and uptime monitoring

## Purpose
Catch a breaking theme/app change before it ships, and catch a live outage or slow degradation within minutes instead of at the next scheduled hygiene sweep.

## Steps
1. Map the store's critical paths (home, PDP, filter, cart, discount code, checkout, login) into test cases.
2. Run visual diffs across breakpoints and scripted end-to-end flows before and after every deploy, plus nightly.
3. Self-heal a test whose selector changed for a cosmetic reason; flag the ones that fail for a real reason.
4. On failure, capture video replay, console errors and a network trace, and write an actionable bug report.
5. Run synthetic checks every few minutes on home, PDP, cart, checkout and search from more than one region.
6. Run a full transaction walk (add-to-cart through confirmation) on a schedule, not just a page-200 check.
7. Track SSL and DNS separately, and pull real-user page-load data to catch slow-but-not-down degradation.
8. Route any failure or degradation to a human with an escalation path if unacknowledged, logging detect and fix time.

## Checks
- No deploy ships without a green regression run.
- Every incident logs a real detect time and fix time.

## Output
A pass/fail regression report with visual diffs and bug replays, plus an uptime dashboard and incident log.

## Example
"Nightly regression: checkout flow failed on Safari mobile after a tag-manager update. Video replay + network trace attached. Deploy blocked until fixed."

# Speed measurement, baseline and monitoring

## Purpose
Measure real page speed honestly, fix the page paid traffic actually lands on first, and keep a running budget so nothing regresses silently.

## Steps
1. Record every response of the real page with speed_lab.record before changing anything.
2. Measure 3 runs on a throttled mobile profile (Pixel 5, slow 4G, 4x CPU) and take the median.
3. Cross-check a suspicious lab result against PageSpeed Insights field data.
4. Fix the page paid ads land on before any other template.
5. Turn every diagnosed fix into a brief: what, needs, tradeoff, who, a numeric pass threshold, and a one-step rollback.
6. Re-audit monthly holding a page-weight and script-count budget, flagging the moment a budget is crossed.
7. Wait about 28 days of field data before calling a fix a win.
8. Before a known sale, list at-risk dynamic steps, load-test them, and freeze risky changes during the window.

## Checks
- Every measurement is 3 runs averaged, never 1.
- Field and lab data are read as separate things, never conflated.
- Every brief's threshold is a number, never a feeling.

## Output
A baseline measurement file, a diagnosis, a developer brief per fix, a monthly trend report, and (seasonally) a peak-readiness report.

## Example
"PDP LCP: 4.1s baseline (median of 3 runs). Fix: preload hero image, cut a blocking script. Threshold: LCP under 2.5s. Rollback: remove the preload tag, one line."
